title: Index of Suspicion
abstract: An 11-year-old boy comes to the emergency department in the evening complaining of pain in the left lower quadrant (LLQ) of his abdomen that has been present all day, is worsening, and now radiates to his back. The pain is sharp and stabbing and is aggravated by walking and stretching, but not by deep breathing. Positioning and rest do not relieve the pain. He has had one soft stool today and denies vomiting, fever, dysuria, cough, and trauma.On physical examination, the boy is afebrile and has a pulse of 102 beats/min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 116/68 mm Hg. There is tenderness on deep palpation in the LLQ as well as rebound tenderness. No psoas or obturator signs are detected, and bowel sounds are normal. Rectal examination does not cause abdominal pain, and the stool is negative for occult blood. No back or scrotal tenderness is present. The remainder of the physical findings are normal.His white blood cell count is 8.1×103/mcL (8.1×109/L), amylase level is 54 U/L, and blood glucose level is 92 mg/dL (5.1 mmol/L). Electrolyte and liver function levels are normal. Urinalysis is negative for nitrites and leukocyte esterase and shows 3 to 5 leukocytes and 1 to 3 erythrocytes per high-power field. Abdominal radiography documents a normal gas pattern and a moderate amount of fecal matter.The patent is admitted and given intravenous fluids. He awakens when the LLQ is palpated. Abdominal ultrasonography shows normal findings. Further imaging leads to a diagnosis.A 10-year-old boy comes to your office because of a painful right eye. He had been well until his mother noticed him rubbing his right eye and having difficulty opening it because of the pain. The boy denies any trauma and otherwise is asymptomatic, having no fever, sore throat, or joint pain. He has been busy taking care of his pets.His physical findings are unremarkable except for the presence of blepharospasm of the right eye. He is difficult to examine because he is unable to keep the lid of the right eye open. Ophthalmologic examination and consultation determine the cause of this patient’s symptoms.A 2-year-old girl is seen in December on the fifth day of a febrile illness that began with vomiting. On the third day, she had developed an erythematous, maculopapular, blanching rash of the trunk, extremities, palms, and soles. Cultures were obtained, and she was treated with antibiotics. Over the following 2 days, she developed diarrhea and lethargy and then was found to be hyponatremic and thrombocytopenic. She was treated with ceftriaxone and transferred to the regional tertiary care center. She lives in eastern North Carolina and attends child care. Her parents deny any exposure to ticks.Physical examination reveals an alert but irritable, ill-appearing girl whose temperature is 101.8°F (38.8°C), heart rate is 140 beats/min, respiratory rate is 40 breaths/min, and blood pressure is 62/32 mm Hg. Her skin is warm, and there is a maculopapular rash on the distal extremities as well as petechiae in the antecubital fossae; the capillary refill is prolonged. Her mouth is dry but clear. Her neck is supple. A cardiac gallop rhythm is present, her lungs are clear, and her abdomen is slightly distended, diffusely tender, and devoid of bowel sounds.Her hemoglobin level is 9.9 g/dL (99 g/L), platelets are 20×103/mcL (20×109/L), and white blood cell count is 3.9×103/mcL (3.9×109/L), with 82% neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, and 3% monocytes. The serum sodium level is 123 mEq/L (123 mmol/L), bicarbonate is 18 mEq/L (18 mmol/L), and glucose is 242 mg/dL (13.4 mmol/L). Stool is positive for occult blood. Findings on urinalysis, electrocardiography, and abdominal radiography are normal.Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and rectal contrast showed a localized infiltration of blood or edema fluid into the fat between the colon and the abdominal wall muscle in the LLQ, just below the level of the iliac crest. The findings were consistent with epiploic appendagitis (EA).The family and patient were educated and reassured about this condition. The boy was discharged from the hospital to follow up with his pediatrician in 1 week. The abdominal pain resolved in 1 month with no complications.The epiploic appendages are located along the colon and are outpouchings composed of both fat and blood vessels. They run along the serosal surface, from the cecum to the rectosigmoid junction, and vary in thickness and length. Among their functions are carrying out local defense against infection (similar to the omentum), storing fat, and acting as a cushion against peristalsis or as a reservoir for blood when there is contraction. EA is caused by an ischemic event that is believed to result from either torsion of the epiploic appendage or spontaneous venous thrombosis.A similar condition, segmental omental infarction (OI), is hypothesized also to be caused by vascular compromise, either from increased abdominal pressure or postprandial vascular congestion. The susceptibility to infarction is high because the blood supply of the omentum is prone to insult. It is embryonic in nature, can be supplied by one or two arteries, and is drained by one vein.Torsion of an appendage is the most common cause of EA. Keeping in mind that EA and OI are diagnoses of exclusion, the incidence is more common in males and is not associated with any particular ethnic group, lifestyle, or genetic pattern. The adult literature states that the condition is more common in the fourth and fifth decades of life. Pediatric data suggest that the structure of fat in children younger than 2 years of age might be protective, although patients as young as 2 years have experienced EA.There are several approaches to developing a differential diagnosis for abdominal pain. When the history and physical findings suggest a specific location for the pain, an anatomic approach can be useful. In this case, the clinician must consider systems in the LLQ, including gastrointestinal (GI), genitourinary (GU), and musculoskeletal. Had the patient been female, a gynecologic disorder would have to be considered.The GI structure in the LLQ is colon. The most common cause of pain in this area is constipation, which can present with a wide spectrum of discomfort patterns. Inflammatory bowel disease, as well as inflammation of an appendix located to the left of the midline, must be considered. Less common are internal hernias.GU pathology includes renal stones, which classically produce a severe, colicky pain that is felt in the flank. Musculoskeletal injuries consist of abdominal wall strains and tears that present as more superficial pain. Disorders affecting females include diseases of the ovary or fallopian tube, such as torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, and ruptured ovarian cyst. Pain localizing to the right lower quadrant produces a similar list of possibilities, although appendicitis is much more likely.Distinguishing between EA and OI is impossible clinically. Both may present similarly with a gradual onset. Most often, the patient does not appear ill, is afebrile, does not complain of nausea and vomiting, and has normal bowel movements and an unchanged appetite. The pain can range from dull to sharp and can be colicky or constant. It usually is localized, and palpation can elicit rebound tenderness. EA is more common on the left side. The pain may begin after an increase in intra-abdominal pressure, such as caused by coughing, deep inhalation, or stretching.Laboratory results usually are unremarkable and should prompt the clinician to consider this diagnosis by exclusion. Computed tomography and ultrasonography can help to confirm the diagnosis. The lesion of EA generally is small and prone to developing a thickened rim of visceral peritoneum, which is referred to as the “ring sign.” The lesion resulting from OI is larger and has a greater mass effect on the adjacent bowel wall. It lacks the ring sign.If the clinical findings and results of imaging convince the clinician that EA or OI is likely and disorders requiring surgery are excluded, a conservative approach is appropriate. There may be situations in which laparotomy may be necessary to resolve the diagnostic dilemma.Surgical ligation is the treatment when the diagnosis results from exploratory laparotomy. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the mainstay of therapy, along with education and support, when the condition is diagnosed without surgery. Potential sequelae include obstruction, intussusception, abscess formation, fever, anorexia, and obstipation.A patient who presents with abdominal pain forces the clinician to construct a long differential list of conditions. A comprehensive history and thorough physical examination help to narrow the diagnostic possibilities and should focus any further diagnostic testing. Imaging can assist in making the diagnosis, especially when a specific process is suspected. When a patient is found to have EA or OI, which are diagnoses made by exclusion with corroboration by imaging, pain relief, education, and encouragement constitute appropriate therapy.After topical anesthetic was administered, the boy’s eyes could be examined. Multiple fine hairs were noted on the eyelid, and the conjunctiva was hyperemic on the right. The left eye was normal. A slitlamp examination revealed tiny spinous processes protruding from the right cornea. Examination of the anterior chamber revealed cells (1+) and flare (1+). On further questioning, it was discovered that “caring for his pets” included walking the dog and cleaning the cage of his pet tarantula. Because the child had been in contact with a tarantula and hairlike projections were found protruding from his cornea that produced a keratouveitis (inflammation of the cornea and iris), ophthalmia nodosa secondary to tarantula hairs was diagnosed.Ophthalmia nodosa is a term used initially to describe granulomatous conjunctivitis caused by caterpillar hairs; the term has been expanded to include ocular inflammation arising from a host of arthropod hairs and stingers or even plant hairs. Ophthalmia nodosa secondary to tarantula hairs has been described in patients having casual contact with tarantulas.Tarantulas are known to fling tiny hairs purposefully off of their bodies toward potential predators by using their rear legs. These hairs are located predominantly on the tarantula’s abdomen. On gross examination they appear soft and velvety. Microscopically, they are noted to be tiny daggers covered with multiple barbs that are capable of penetrating several cell layers.Parents and children who may become owners of one of these creatures should be warned about the potential dangers when handling a tarantula or cleaning the cage. The skin, as well as the eyes, can be affected by contact with the arthropod. Both urticaria and papular dermatitis secondary to tarantula hair contact are other known consequences of tarantula exposure. A tarantula also may inflict injury by biting, causing painful physical trauma with its fangs as well as a chemical reaction from envenomation.The differential diagnosis of an acutely reddened eye in a child is lengthy. If pain is present, the list narrows considerably.Infectious causes of the red eye include infections with viruses, bacteria, fungi, Chlamydia, and protozoa. Of the acute viral etiologies, adenovirus is the most common. Recent exposure to conjunctivitis as well as signs and symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection suggest viral conjunctivitis. Although these entities cause redness and sometimes the sensation of a foreign body in the eye, photophobia, and discharge, rarely are they painful. Bacterial conjunctivitis is associated with purulent discharge and can cause significant hyperemia, but it also rarely causes pain unless an ulcer is present.Allergic conjunctivitis generally is characterized by itchiness, redness, swelling, and bilateral involvement, although the clinical picture can vary. Again, pain is not an issue. The diagnosis depends substantially on the history.Uveitis and glaucoma also are considerations, but in the absence of historical risk factors (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis or previous trauma), these conditions are highly unlikely in children. The uveitis of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis usually is not painful. Acute narrow-angle glaucoma in adults is extremely painful but is essentially nonexistent in children.The presence of pain in addition to hyperemia suggests another group of disorders. Bacterial, herpetic, or protozoan (Acanthamoeba) ulcers can be very painful. Traumatic injuries such as corneal abrasion, blunt force contusion, missile injury, or penetrating injury should be considered, even in the absence of a specific history. Children are notorious for denying any knowledge of the circumstances of eye trauma initially.Ferrous and other inorganic corneal foreign bodies are common sources of acute eye pain and redness. Because these foreign bodies may be small or lodged under the upper lid, eversion of the upper lid is mandatory, and sometimes slitlamp examination is required.Contact lens overwear or tight contact lens syndrome can cause redness and pain. Contact lens use is known to be a risk factor for infectious ulcers, which can be very painful. Chemical injury to the eye, such as with household cleaning solutions, which the patient may deny initially, is another cause of ocular inflammation and can be painful.Lid disorders such as chalazion, hordeolum, blepharitis, or louse infestation of the lashes rarely cause pain. Cellulitis of the lids or periorbital tissues can be painful but usually is obvious.In the absence of a clear-cut history to explain the red, painful eye, referral for evaluation to an ophthalmologist is indicated.Treatment of ophthalmia nodosa requires the administration of topical steroids and removal of the hairs, if possible. The prognosis varies, depending on the species of the tarantula and the degree of involvement. Continued evaluation by an ophthalmologist is essential to ensure adequate resolution of the eye inflammation once the tarantula hairs have been removed.Spider bites typically occur when the insect is trapped, threatened, or crushed against the skin. Diagnosis may be difficult because the spider rarely is seen or recovered. Although all spiders have the ability to inflict painful bites, only a few are medically significant for their bites, the two most important being the brown recluse spider (Loxosceles sp) and the black widow spider (Latrodectus sp).The brown recluse spider is common in the midwestern and southeastern United States. Although most bites are asymptomatic, there can be both local and systemic manifestations. Necrotic skin changes can occur 72 to 96 hours after the bite. Envenomation can result in the systemic condition known as loxoscelism, which results in minimal skin changes but massive hemolysis.The black widow spider bite is a worldwide problem that results predominately in local pain, irritation, and at times latrodectism, the systemic form. Black widow bites do not produce marked skin changes. Symptoms include muscle cramping, pain, and other neuromuscular-related problems. Antivenin is available and successful in relieving the effect of latrodectism, but should be reserved for very severe cases.Although tarantulas are native to a relatively small geographic region, their recent increase in popularity as pets means that pediatricians everywhere may have patients who have tarantulas in their homes. Parents look to pediatricians for advice on a variety of issues. Recommendations on whether a tarantula is an appropriate or safe pet for a child must take into consideration the natural tendencies and defense mechanisms of the animal as well as the consequences of exposure to and handling of them.Meningococcemia, bacterial meningitis, toxic shock syndrome, viral encephalopathy, infectious mononucleosis, rickettsial diseases, endocarditis, syphilis, atypical Kawasaki disease, and intra-abdominal processes were considered as causes of this child’s clinical presentation.Therapy with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, doxycycline, acyclovir, and vasopressors was initiated, along with fluid resuscitation. The patient was intubated because of progressive respiratory distress. title: Cyberfangs: online Communities and the Gothic Hypercharacter
abstract: This chapter attempts to analyse the social and cultural values that are being communicated, or implicated, by these cake choices, and explore how the seductive qualities of the Gothic genre, when combined with the sudden influx of frighteningly apocalyptic visions, presents a challenge to the traditional ideas and function of a wedding cake. Connecting the Gothic to wedding cakes can transgress boundaries by demonstrating what is outside the proper 'contours of the world'. Many of the cakes feature a topper that has the bride and groom as skeletons in fancy dress marked with the texts, 'Love Never Dies' or 'Til death do us part'. Other cakes feature spider webs carved into the icing; mould, overgrown moss, and detritus; coffins; eyeballs and disembodied hands; and beetles and bugs, all attempting to paint a very vivid picture of death and decay. They are compelling and captivating due to the atypical and distinctive nature of the expression, which subvert wedding cake traditions.

title: Maria Sibylla Merian and Bobbi Wilson: Challenging Inequality Through A Love of Entomology
abstract: An enchanting blend of plants and insects in Maria Sibylla Merian’s botanical illustration, circa 1720. Amidst the vast realms of the natural world, a microcosmos teeming with arthropod secrets exists—a world of vibrant colors, intricate patterns, and extraordinary adaptations. When the insect kingdom beckoned, one remarkable woman, Maria Sybilla Merian (1647–1717), dared to venture into their hidden universe and study their lifestyles and interactions with other living creatures. From cultivating silkworms as a young teenager to studying insect morphology and metamorphosis in Suriname, Merian was a force of nature whose seminal works helped to systemically deconstruct scientific dogma and found the discipline of entomology. (Left): Maria Sibylla Merian (Right): Bobbi Wilson (Photo by Andrew Hurley, Yale University Born on 2 April 1647 in Frankfurt, Germany, Merian was just three years of age when her father, Matthäus Merian, a renowned engraver, died (Rogers 2023). Despite Matthäus’s death early in Maria’s life, the Merian family’s artistic legacy would live on. Merian’s extraordinary drawing ability as a young child was noted by her stepfather, Jacob Marrel, an eminent German painter, who nurtured her abilities and provided her with teachers in his atelier throughout her childhood (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Maria Sibylla Merian made foundational scientific discoveries, developed robust methods for entomology through conducting field research, and pursued ecological endeavors of great scientific importance for entomology. Her work was initially often overlooked as merely a piece of early natural philosophy. However, beginning in the 1970s and subsequent studies of scholarship in the 1980s and 1990s, a re-examination of her work, its originality, and her innovative approach and findings helped establish her pivotal role in laying the foundation for the modern field of entomology, and consequently inspired people of all ages to explore the natural world (Valiant 1992, 1993; Heard 2020). Merian’s descriptions of metamorphosis and her refutation of scientific concepts that had been long entrenched in society played a significant role in bolstering her scientific reputation. Making discoveries and disproving widely accepted scientific beliefs was not always positively received. During Merian’s lifetime, people generally accepted Aristotle’s theory of spontaneous generation, which held that living things could spring from nonliving matter. Scientists and laypeople did not realize that all insects produce eggs and thought that some insects just “spontaneously” grew out of garbage and detritus (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Through Merian’s intensive observation, illustration, and ultimate discovery, she “saw each stage in a bug’s life cycle as a continuous process, when few other naturalists were making connections” between the caterpillar and the butterfly (Swaby 2018; Fig. 1). Merian’s fundamental scientific research on metamorphosis was a nail in the coffin of the antiquated belief in spontaneous generation. Metamorphosis of the Silkworm, Maria Sibylla Merian, 1679. (Wikimedia Commons.) CONSTANTLY SURROUNDED BY PLANTS, INSECTS, AND OTHER ANIMALS, IN ADDITION TO RECEIVING EXPLANATIONS AND WISDOM FROM THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLE, MERIAN WITNESSED THE INTERCONNECTEDNESS OF ECOSYSTEMS WITH A NEW PERSPECTIVE As a result, Merian’s lifetime of field research and artistic study paved the way for the creation of essential scientific methods. At thirteen years old, Merian did not have the resources to fuel her curious mind. No books correctly explained the transitional processes she was observing in insects. She had to conduct her own research, grow her own insects, and generate her own unique hypotheses about insect development (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). To conduct studies, Merian “situated her specimens in context, capturing them crawling on leaves with curing seams, flying over flowers’ stretching tendrils, or circling around stems,” (Swaby 2018). Merian’s distinct approach to scientific observation through an artistic lens set her apart from other illustrators of the time, who solely worked from display cases. She took scrupulous notes and recorded her observations with detailed written descriptions, drawings, and paintings, all of which solidified her live observational methodologies (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018, Beck 2007). Enabled by her home caterpillar farm, Merian drew “pictures in her study book that reflected not only what animals and plants looked like but how they developed” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian’s observations were limited by her own eyes and occasionally looking through a magnifying glass, as microscopy was just beginning to emerge as its own field. With this minimal available technology, the connections Merian made among plants, insects, and animals highlight how much can be learned from careful observations and meticulous record-keeping, further raising the bar for today’s entomologists, who have much more sophisticated tools at their disposal. Merian’s search for opportunities to expand her understanding of the insect world led her to pursue research abroad that set her apart from other naturalists. Merian was “astounded to see what lovely creatures were brought back from the East and West Indies” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). These species of animals native to South America sparked her interest, so, in June of 1699, Merian, along with her daughter Dorothea, set sail from Amsterdam to Suriname (Rogers 2023). First colonized by the Dutch, Suriname was exploited for its land, and the Indigenous people were forced to work as slaves on plantations that grew sugar, coffee, cocoa, and cotton (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). While many of the colonizers came in search of wealth, Merian was interested in the knowledge that would follow from the exploration of the land’s species. Noting this difference, Merian wrote, “The [Dutch] people there have no desire to investigate such things; indeed they mocked me for seeking something other than sugar in that country” (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). She did not let this cruelty discourage her. With the help of many Indigenous women, Merian and her daughter settled into a home with a quaint garden in the colonies’ capital, Paramaribo, to take on their scientific investigations (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Due to the warm, wet climate, home visits from a diverse collection of vibrant species were common. “Blue lizards laid eggs in the corners of rooms,” “cockroaches that ventured inside were captured for study,” and the garden often welcomed hummingbirds (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Constantly surrounded by plants, insects, and other animals, in addition to receiving explanations and wisdom from the Indigenous people, Merian witnessed the interconnectedness of ecosystems with a new perspective (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). From her two years of consistent observation, Merian was able to publish a collection of watercolor illustrations. As shown in her painting Guava Tree with Huntsman Spider within the collection entitled Insects of Suriname, Merian vividly captured insects, their prey, and the plants in their native tropical environment (Fig. 2). No other scientific artists at the time were publishing work featuring the importance of the interconnectedness between insects and their ecosystems and elucidating predator–prey relationships (Merian 1726). The uniqueness and merit of Merian’s painted illustrations and their corresponding insightful explanations helped her gain access to the male-dominated scientific community. Guava Tree with Huntsman Spider, Orb Weaver Spider, Leaf-Cutter Ants, Army Ants, Cockroach, Tarantulas, and Hummingbird (watercolor). Maria Sibylla Merian, The Insects of Suriname, 1726. Despite the setbacks Merian faced along her scientific and artistic journeys as an orphan, a woman in 17th-century society, and a divorcee, her family’s socioeconomic positioning and national origin meant that she had access to resources that one must consider in the discussion of her success. Although Merian overcame many barriers throughout her artistic and scientific career, her privilege should not go unnoticed. Scientific exploration has been built on the backs of enslaved people, colonization, and Eurocentric ideals. Merian’s access even at a young age to an art studio set her ahead of others interested in discovery. Due to her stepfather’s profession, Merian had an advantage in both her access to artistic education and lessons on scientific observation and note-taking. Women during the 17th century were not allowed to attend art school or universities to formally study science, but Merian had the opportunity to study with her stepfather’s apprentices. She continued to benefit from her family’s wealth into her later life. While Merian “did not approve of the treatment” of the enslaved people, her research in Suriname relied on the traditional knowledge held by Native women regarding the species of insects and plants of the surrounding forests. With the aid of enslaved people, Merian was able to venture into the forest and steer clear of poisonous plants and dangerous animals (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian’s life was spent observing insects and their connections to the environment through art. Unlike many other women at the time, she published her findings in many series of collections such as The Caterpillar Book, volumes one, two, and three (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). In these publications, readers can observe how Merian refined her understanding of insect development and unraveled the interdependencies of living creatures across the tree of life. Beyond her scientific achievements, Merian was cognizant of her great privilege and actively worked to end oppressive systems in the Americas by hiring enslaved people, showing her willingness to confront the small-scale challenges of the emerging field of entomology as well as the large-scale problems facing society (Pomeroy and Kathirithamby 2018). Merian entered the scientific world as a young German girl trying to explore the natural world through an artistic lens. However, she transformed the scientific community with her curiosity for the insect world, and her legacy lives on through the fresh young minds exploring the possibilities of scientific discovery at their fingertips. A modern-day Merian named Bobbi Wilson has recently emerged from her own chrysalis. Wilson’s intrepid curiosity about spotted lanternflies and the insect world has helped her gracefully transcend the barriers of race and gender that sought to extinguish her emerging interests in entomology at the young age of nine (Poitras 2023). While Merian’s full life came to an end centuries ago, her legacy lives on, and Bobbi Wilson’s life in science is just beginning to unfold. Top: Bobbi Wilson labelling lanternflies. Bottom: Bobbi Wilson and her parents (Both photos by Andrew Hurley, Yale University). ALTHOUGH BORN FOUR CENTURIES APART, CONSIDERATION OF MERIAN AND WILSON HIGHLIGHTS THE RACIAL AND GENDER INEQUALITIES THAT STILL PLAGUE SCIENCE TODAY. Reflecting on Merian’s life and her passion for arthropods shines a light on the story of Bobbi Wilson, a young Black girl with a fascination for spotted lanternflies, who was wrongfully reported to local police by a neighbor while harvesting specimens from the sidewalk of her neighborhood (Poitras 2023). This report was an overt act of racism. Bobbi, a 9-year-old girl, was reported as an adult Black woman by a White neighbor, Gordon Lawshe. It was stated that “Lawshe saw something scary. Recognizing it was not an emergency per se, he called the police department dispatcher instead. ‘There’s a little Black woman walking, spraying stuff on the sidewalks and trees on Elizabeth and Florence,’ Lawshe told the dispatcher. ‘I don’t know what the hell she’s doing. Scares me, though,’ Lawshe added” (Romo 2023). The adultification of young Black children has been a dangerously common practice across the United States and still persists today. Racial profiling puts children at risk for trauma and police violence. While the police officers involved handled the situation calmly, the experience is extremely impactful at a personal and societal level, as it shows the obstacles a Black girl encounters while following her passion for science. Although born four centuries apart, consideration of Merian and Wilson highlights the racial and gender inequalities that still plague science today. Both Merian and Wilson remind us that scientific discovery is attainable and literally right at one’s doorstep if one has an inquisitive mind and determined spirit, but hurdles persist. Challenging 17th-century scientific tenets or being a young Black girl showing interest in science in the 21st century can be seen as threatening by some members of society. Today, individuals at scientific institutions must all actively strive to break down structural inequities in scientific education and make scientific discovery a more accessible and inclusive space. The author would like to thank Lawrence Gall, Ph.D., for discussions, Jennifer Barrer-Gall and Kelly Morrow for reading the manuscript and helpful suggestions, and Stephen Lory, Ph.D., for encouraging journal submission.

title: Parallelism Enhancing Cellular Communication - on Knowledge City Evolving
venue: World Congress on Intelligent Control and Automation
abstract: The knowledge and information infrastructure, especially its health and security protection being not negotiated, can be related for national development, and evidenced in traditional Chinese shuyuans being as knowledge centers. To evolve contemporary knowledge economy, holistic, inclusive, information interactions are getting more importance. Plural (dual) surveillance which is rooted in biologic senses, e.g., from two-eyes, can have the feature of fault-tolerance, availability and maintainability in monitoring tasks. It can fit the contemporary wireless communication methods being incorporated with MIMO (multi-in multi-out), to prevent information loss, interference, unexpected changes caused by such as clogged water. Network prototypes, including SW (spider-web) and CCC (cube-connected cycle) networks, are proactively suggested for evolving information based development. Furthermore, the mutually independent Hamiltonian Path (MIHP) property of SW can be used for parallel analyzing interference and supporting cypher coding to offer privacy. Similarly, other networks, such as the Honeycomb tori, can offer an alternative pattern.

title: Biomimetic and bio‑inspired multispectral stealth materials: Design strategies, fabrication, and radar infrared performance
abstract: Biomimetic and bio-inspired approaches offer a promising route to next-generation multispectral stealth by combining structure-driven electromagnetic (EM) wave control with materials-level thermal regulation. This review synthesizes recent advances in biomimetic radar and infrared-stealth materials, focusing on biological design principles, fabrication strategies, EM- and IR-loss mechanisms, and multifunctional integration. We first summarize the theoretical basis of radar cross-section reduction and IR signature suppression, then categorize key bio-inspired motifs-moth-eye, lotus-leaf, spider-web, honeycomb, plant-derived and other hierarchical structures and discuss how each modulates scattering, impedance matching, multiple internal reflection, interfacial/dipolar polarization and conductive/magnetic loss to achieve broadband microwave absorption. Next, we review IR-stealth strategies inspired by polar bear fur, Saharan silver ants, cephalopods and other organisms for thermal insulation, emissivity control and adaptive camouflage. Representative fabrication methods-hydrothermal, electrospinning, templating, 3D printing, freeze-drying, CVD and metamaterial patterning and common compositional platforms including carbonaceous materials, MXenes, conductive polymers, ferrites and nanocomposites are compared with emphasis on process–structure–function links. We highlight examples of multifunctional stealth materials that simultaneously deliver low radar cross-section, reduced IR emissivity, mechanical robustness, superhydrophobicity and lightweight design. Finally, we identify current challenges-multispectral compatibility, environmental durability, thickness/weight constraints, and scalable manufacturing and propose future directions for integrated material structural optimization and active/adaptive stealth systems. This comprehensive review provides design guidelines and a roadmap for developing high-performance biomimetic multispectral stealth materials for aerospace, naval and wearable applications.

title: Lion City
abstract: Lion City Ng Yi-Sheng (bio) On our third date, we went to the Zoo. “I’ll show you where we make the animals,” she slurred, still tipsy from the Carlsberg. It was three a.m., but she was the hottest thing I’d ever laid my eyes or hands on, so I said sure, why the hell not, let’s go. We zipped down Mandai Road on her chili-red Yamaha motorbike, me tapping her helmet every five minutes to keep her awake, past walls and walls of choke-thick jungle: a mess of flame of the forest and jelutong. I hadn’t been to see the animals since primary school, so I’d forgotten about this bit of Singapore: a piece of wild left over from before the skyscrapers and bonsai gardens swallowed everything up. We got to the alphabetized parking lot, slipped past the entryway, where all the tourist info desks and the orangutan-themed café lay dark and silent. Then we came to an iron door painted with zebra stripes. She waved her card at an RFID scanner and pulled me in. “This is where the magic happens,” she whispered, sticking her tongue in my ear. And no joke, when I’m in her presence I think with my lower half every second on the clock, but the sight before me goggled my eyes so hard, sex was the last thing on my brain. We were in a warehouse filled top to bottom with animals on shelves. Tigers and tapirs and tamarins, cheek by jowl, squatting still next to each other like so many library books. Life-sized beasts—and no toy-shop reproductions either: in the dark I could hear them breathing, yipping, whooping even, their jet-black eyes winking in the light of my Samsung screen. She laughed at my slack-jawed stupor. “This never gets old,” she said, and ducked into the shadows, leaving me alone with the thousand-odd animals. Seconds later, she popped up again with a flashlight in her left hand and a something in her right. “Look,” she said. Flanked by pillars of possums and penguins, the something wasn’t impressive: just a pawful of wire mesh, cable spaghetti and the like, silicon garbage, the city’s detritus. But then she tickled it under its chin—yes, it had a chin—and it stretched its arms and eyes, and yawned and nestled again, buzzing against her breasts, kittenish, puppylike. “Lion cub.” “Huh?” [End Page 58] “I’ve been working on it these past three months. New design for infant lion. Release date’s confirmed: edition of six, just in time for Chinese New Year.” She popped open her purse and pulled out these tiny fuzzy pajama onesies, clenched the flashlight in her teeth, and forced that wriggling little baby robo-cub in. And what do you know, with the bot in those clothes, it really looked like a genuine little Simba, whiskers and all. “Skin,” she told me proudly. “Zoo’s finest achievement. Pulls the wool over their eyes. We could make a toaster look like a tarantula.” “No shit.” But her attention had drifted. “Here, hold this,” she said, and thrust the mewling cub into my hands. I fumbled and it bit me, but I stopped my curse halfway when I saw she was removing her shoes and her T-shirt, her jeans and her socks and her bra. She clambered onto her workbench, her graceful arm clearing a space for us amidst the wires and screws, the flamingo feathers and fox fur. “Come on up,” she grinned. “Let’s make some animals of our own.” I’d met her the way everyone meets these days: on the Internet. She’d liked my profile, she said. It was no fun going out with a bad boy; her hobby was preying on decent, hardworking office types who actually took a bit of effort to corrupt. Other things she liked included punk rock bands, graffiti art, the spicier varieties of Indian food, the most slapstick of Hong Kong kung fu comedies. Anything that was loud and joyous and verging on the borders of good taste. “I didn’t have much...

title: Spiritual (Mal)practice
abstract: Spiritual abuse as tufts of rabbit fur and twine feathered the nest of my familial home. My father was prey to Lutheran missionaries who set up shop on a plot of land belonging to his father in the village of Crabwood Creek, Guyana. To survive decolonization in 1966 and immigration to the United States, the only path he saw included his being devoured by empire’s acting arm: Christianity.The British never imagined Guyana as anything but a place of extraction, never a permanent home for people—but the coolies of the Empire were not yet human, indentured to serve (officially five-year) contracts that bound them to plantations and their economies through pitiful, demeaning wages and reliance on colonial power structures. It would make sense that, to get an education in this rural Indian village, my father had to convert to Christianity, at least nominally, to go to the missionaries’ school, where he learned—though perhaps not explicitly—that his own home traditions were backward, the antithesis of sophistication.He converted fully after another brush with forced conversion in 1984 in New York City, where Lutherans provided us, our family of five, with enough food to last another brutal winter. My mother, then, allowed white Americans to “witness” to her and for the sake of survival in the United States blended her beliefs into a syncretic form of Christianity.This is the backdrop for my own explorations into the generational healing that I struggle with. Relearning language. Relearning religion. Relearning spirituality that always felt to be on the horizon of my own personal self-discovery.. . .आज तू वक़्त के चुनरिया छोड़ेलाइ अच्छी रंग-विरंगी रेसमियाइ बदन के भी छोड़ेला।कांपत-कांपत डरो मततू दुसर किनारा पहुंचके समझबा।. . .DevotionWaking up at five a.m. to read the bible.Washing your hands and feet before lighting incense.Filial pietyमातृ देवो भव।पितृ देवो भव।आचार्य देवो भव।अितिथ देवो भव॥Saying the right pronunciation.Having the right color skin.Praying for the right colored skin so that God can hear.Believing all your ancestors are burning in Hell.Rightness of action, speech, being.Being of a caste that is allowed to touch the statue’s feet.Being of a caste that is allowed to chant in Sanskrit.. . .Sarai Rohilla, Delhi (2002)कहाँ से आया कहाँ जाओगेखबर करो अपने तन से—Prahlad TipaniyaThree men huddle close over cards and rupee notesthough it’s summer of 46 C. Orange light overhead,the almost deserted platform burns its coil cold. May I haveyour attention please. The train on platform two is a cowand the tracks are the underworld’s riverbefore it silts and snakes into old age. It’s older than you think.In the distance trumpets and a brahmin asking for 2,500 rupeesto ensure your father’s spirit does not starve. The mosquitoesin your berth aren’t hungry. You have seen to it personally.They leave their poisoned saliva under your skin. You will knowexactly where they have been. Delhi could be Jaipur could beBenares, could be New York City. Your body is of planks and steelin need of filling and repair. The tracks are alreadywhere they are going. One track of veins goes andone track of arteries comes. What exactly can you see of this,friend, looking desperately for a destination with your head up your ass?. . .I grew up hearing chutney music and music in Bhojpuri, though, without my Aji as decoder, the access to the ideas and theorizing the universe remained occluded. A colonial caul. A shield against what our bodies knew intuitively through drum and dance. Through movement I came to realization first. (We are not of caste identity that would be recognized in India—of those able to learn the Vedas or to chant in Sanskrit.)Kabir, the bhakti poet of medieval South Asia, migrated with jahajees into the Caribbean with my family. The thing about Kabir, as Arvind Krishna Mehrotra, translator of Songs of Kabir says, is that Kabir is more of a spirit anyway. That the authenticity of the penned verse relies on the kavi chhap, the poet’s signature line, कहत कबीर सुनो भाई साधो Says Kabir, listen wise brothersHis work is collected in three main volumes: the Bijak of Kabir in Bhojpuri, the Guru Granth Sahib in Punjabi, and Rajasthani manuscripts. In all these versions Kabir emerges as a poet who fervently decries caste, religious difference, and any kind of division that people create between one another.The first Kabir poem I learned was through Babla and Kanchan performing the Yusuff Khan song “Aaj Sawaliya.” When I learned the meaning of the song, it crashed on me with awakening. I sat in a restaurant in Jackson Heights and translated and retranslated and retranslated the song from Bhojpuri into English into Creole into Bhojpuri for at least twenty iterations so that each iteration contained a different aspect of the magic Kabir sang about, each incarnation of the song became its own diaspora of the original, which was of dubious origins anyway.I must be comfortable immersed in the Unknown.. . .Today you leave behind everything you knoweven time’s veileven that this body is made of living mattereven this body.Do not be afraid (though you tremble)you will understand from the other side of knowing.. . .On the other hand, my Nani—my mother’s mother—grew up as a Christian just outside Georgetown, and when she wed my Nana she was made to convert to Hinduism. Her own family was a mix of Christians with roots in South India at least two generations back. Her name Emma was changed to Amla.When she died my mother dreamed her singing “Onward Christian Soldiers,” which was haunting in various directions. She sat on a swing and told my mother, “Believe what they say about Jesus.”Missionization. Forced conversion. Patriarchal control. Spiritual abuse. Violence.I learned to play the hymn on the saxophone when I was thirteen and played it in the Southern Baptist church closest to my home in Chuluota, Florida. I cherish the part of the song that reminds me of her and her spirit—free to visit us now in the form of cardinals.But questions of the origin of my name burned itself into my heart. I was not allowed to ask questions. My father insisted a little education is a dangerous thing. I think he meant it was dangerous to look back at the plantation and try to divine wisdom.. . .I learned to pray the Lord’s Prayer. I learned the Lutheran liturgy. While I know this by heart and can sing it, it comes from the Luther Book of Worship.kyrieP: In peace, let us pray to the Lord.C: Lord, have mercy.P: For the peace from above, and for our salvation, let us pray to the Lord.C: Lord, have mercy.P: For the peace of the whole world, for the well-being of the Church of God, and for the unity of all, let us pray to the Lord.C: Lord, have mercy.P: For this Holy House, and for all who offer here their worship and praise, let us pray to the Lord.C: Lord, have mercy.P: Help, save, comfort, and defend us, gracious Lord.C: Amen.Ritual that leads to realization? For some? For anyone? For my ancestors burning in hell?. . .The Greatest of TheseI’ve only ever knownthat God is lovea few times like thismorning fillingthe coffee pot, the windblowing the birch leavesand crab apples intothe holes my dog clawedafter the rain, and howlooking at the work I needto do in the yard,I smile at her joy atsmelling the forthcoming rain,my throwing the uprootedtree dendrite into the clouds;and how I am back,looking out from the window,shocked into my breathmy body: the damholding up love to Godas if everything betweenis blending into the lightof the coffee maker,and then there is no dam—And isn’t it just so easyto believe that every last thingis doomed insteadof letting this knowingwash over you and allowingthe deluge to carve new canyonsand gorges as your spine,pushing through the muck of you(which is love too)and flowing from your crownand down your neck andflooding the entire earth,until you return to the earth,which is to say you returnto another of your selves,that grasps at the memoryof being that conduitthat almost had you weepingon the linoleum tilesnot for grief or joy or anythingthat you can name, butfor finally knowing, reallyknowing, you are birch,you are apple, river, dam—. . .Dogma does not serve. After unlearning hell and divine punishment, after a BA in religious studies to relearn mantras, I developed my own sadhana—a practice of daily rituals to ground me into remembering my Aji, my Nani, my ancestors.I learned what I could from the mantras of my Aji’s and my mother’s sadhana, those prayers that I pray are coded in Sanskrit to Brahma, Vishnu, Maheshwara, Sakshat, and so on, but are really aimed at my ancestors, and the gods of this land that I am on, whose names I do not know except for the tingle I get when I hear the peaks sing to me.There are two types of bhakti poetry, classically: the sagun, those poems and songs dedicated to the gods who take forms that we recognize; and the nirgun, those poems and songs dedicated to the God whose form is unseen and Unknown.I chant the names of Unknown through the languages of the ocean, the water cycle, the earth, the mountain, the air.. . .You resamawa ke orhnia chamke chamkein de sun.Hear you neighbah talk,Wha kine slackness—?You stap sing a Kabir bhajan.Na worried.De an‘ all mus‘ go.. . .My mother has been divorced from my father for thirteen years now. That was a challenge for her, for me, for my brother, for my sister. What it meant was going against the Sita-Savitri promise of the patriarchy that bound her—that binds us all. We don’t divorce, was the subconscious message from my mother, and the overt message from her father was, Men do these things and you just have to deal with them.My mother’s conversion story is the same: forced conversion by Lutherans who in Ridgewood gave us food our first winter in this cold country.In the summer I moved to Boulder, my brother had fallen through the floorboards and into some land, his spirit stolen by spirits and adultery. My mother wanted to bless her new home, particularly the fifteen-by-ten room where my brother lived. He moved in with her after his separation from my sister-in-law. I wrote bless when I meant cleanse.She asked me to recite the Hanuman Chalisa with her and to walk around the house with burning incense and a diya, inviting the light back into the windows and the walls. We did it, marking our foreheads in vermillion, and marking the forehead of my brother’s youngest son. In this moment, the devotion that we showed was to the Pratima—that picture of the Monkey God that we are named after (Mohabir)—but more sincerely to our older ways of being in the world. For my mother this meant remembering her ancestors—her mother and father.The forty verses to Hanuman written by the bhakti (devotional poet) Tulsidas, the Hanuman Chalisa, was the very prayer my mother recited when her mother died, and also one of the Hindu prayers she taught me.She is seeking out a pastor, an obeah man, a pandit to cry mantras into the wind and earth to heal this fault line in our family.. . .avadhū, māyā tajī na jāyWhat marks you read as mantrasis Maya—not gold orb-weaver,but black scratches your mindhears as sound. Pull out the garnetof your breast at midnight.Does it glint red without sun?The riverbed awaits your salts.After burning into nitrogen andcarbon dioxide, bone fragmentserupt from ash, are called pearls—untouched gems you will neverfinger as prayer beads chantingthe rote in search of god. Selah,have you ever known your body?. . .I have started to take Rabindranath Tagore’s translations of Kabir and retranslate them into my own language, using my own ideals of what the Divine is for me. My spirit leaps at anti-divisive philosophy and reminds me that our language makes us think in binaries, how translation even relies on two shores: the original language as one bank, and the target language as the other. I am more interested in the water between—the transit that erases self and submerges caste and creed in its swirl and dark. In that place of the Divine femme: the Dark Goddess that is not named, there is no right performance of puja and prayer. I crave that nakedness, to peel off my shell, to follow it into the next worlds. How to translate this in fixed couplets? Every translation is a mistranslation. Every statement of this spiritual practice is a misstatement.This for me is a process of retranslation when it comes to Tagore’s translations. I use the same title he uses, transliterated from the “original” Kabir poem, and people it with my own symbols and significance. In this way I am reading deeply into Kabir’s philosophies but queering them, reanimating them from nineteenth-century stasis. And this is just a trick of three dimensions: paper, ink, the eye, the interpretation of the linguistic sign—all arbitrary.. . .ghar ghar dīpak baraiI’ll burn in my home,for another thirty years,maybe fewer—the spun cotton of my bodybent before metformin,gemfibrozil, lisinopril.Today may as well be Diwali.I’ve hand-rolled ladoos of gramand ghee. On each one:Heart line, life line, Moundof Venus. I’ve lined upclay vessel after claybody, each red life throwninto the river after sputteringinto black. My headis on fire. I’m still hopingfor a jasmine to openas though a door to my skull,before it explodes on the pyre.I want to see. title: Plasticity and Cognition in Spiders
The Bugs of America 1826–1838
abstract: The first time I saw the original print of John James Audubon’s portrait of the yellow-billed cuckoo from his The Birds of America series (Fig. 1), I was startled by its size. The print is on a sheet of paper that is more than 3 feet by 2 feet, a size of paper known within the printing business as double elephant folio (Fries 1973). Centered on this massive sheet of paper is an image of a male yellow-billed cuckoo apparently squabbling with a female cuckoo with a beautifully rendered tiger swallowtail butterfly grasped in her bill. The birds are maneuvering through the branches of a pawpaw tree that is laden with ripe fruit, with leaves clearly damaged by leaf miners and black spot fungal disease. The level of detail in the image is astounding, and the lifelike postures of the birds leads one to imagine hearing the wooden, staccato ka-ka-ka-ka-ka-kow-kow-kowlp* of the male as he chases his mate through the tree. Even after the 189 years since it was printed, the hand-painted watercolors are still vibrant and exhibit lifelike subtlety in tone and saturation; the fine engraved lines that capture the feather detail are still razor-sharp and clear. Yellow-billed cuckoo with zebra swallowtail butterfly, Plate 2 from Audubon’s The Birds of America. Digital image created from Clara Peck Collection, Transylvania University. I was introduced to Audubon and his prints by B. J. Gooch, the Special Collections Librarian at Transylvania University, where I am a biology professor. Through her encouragement, I began to take my students into the rare book room to look at our original first edition of Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species and to see all of the books written by Alfred Wallace, Darwin’s co-author of the original paper on evolution. Over time, the library tours with my students evolved to include other books and natural history artifacts, ultimately concluding with a dramatic opening of the specially made cabinet that holds the four-volume set of John James Audubon’s magnum opus, the double elephant folio collection of prints titled The Birds of America. As an entomologist, my eye would fix upon the various insects and spiders that Audubon included in his bird portraits. Most striking was that there was often enough detail and accuracy in the engraving that one could easily identify the insect or spider to species, as with the tiger swallowtail in the yellow-billed cuckoo print. After hearing me express my appreciation of the detail in Audubon’s prints, the director of the library encouraged me to identify all of the insects represented in the 435 prints and call the work The Bugs of America. The project ultimately expanded to involve digitally archiving the university’s set of Audubon prints (Fig. 2), because each print is individually hand-painted and each version of an Audubon bird print is unique. I examined each archived print to catalog and identify to the most specific taxonomic level possible all of the insects, spiders, and other terrestrial arthropods represented in the prints. Following on the work of Teale (1947), I then compared each of the final engravings with a facsimile of Audubon’s original paintings, which had been reprinted by the New-York Historical Society (Davidson 1966, Olson 2012). The New-York Historical Society acquired the original paintings when Audubon’s wife, Lucy, sold them in 1863 for $4,000, equivalent to about $1,040,000 today. By comparing the facsimiles of the originals to the final prints, I was able to ascertain which insects were likely drawn by Audubon himself, added later by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr., or painted by other artists who collaborated with Audubon in making the original paintings. Author with student assistant Nikki Fox digitally archiving the original 435 Audubon prints. A special cradle was built to support the binding of the massive books. Photo credit: Susan Brown. As an entomologist, my eye would fix upon the various insects and spiders that Audubon included in his bird portraits. Most people believe that Audubon is the sole artist responsible for an Audubon print, but most of the prints were actually created through a cooperative process with other artists. When I compared the original paintings with the finished prints, I determined that 155 of the 435 prints (36%) are unaltered translations from Audubon’s original painting to the final print. The remainder of the prints either include elements created by other artists Audubon collaborated with, or the final print was altered or finished by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr. During the 12 years in which the prints were created, Audubon employed five different artists, including two of his own sons, to assist in painting the backgrounds. These artists painted the leaves and flowers to represent distinct plant species and to add details such as insects, spiders, and other non-avian animals that would create a sense of place and, at times, drama to the final composition. Because of Audubon’s “idiosyncratic approach to acknowledging assistance” (Lindsay 2018), it is not surprising that most people are unfamiliar with Audubon’s assistants. In the early years of the project (1820–1822), Audubon was assisted by Joseph Mason, an 18-year-old student from Audubon’s drawing school in Cincinnati, Ohio. Joseph Mason traveled with Audubon up and down the Mississippi and Ohio rivers to collect birds and plant specimens and to paint them for Audubon. Mason is thought to have painted 150–200 background watercolors for Audubon, of which Audubon used 56 uncredited (Olson 2012). The other major contributor to Audubon’s prints was Maria Martin, a South Carolinian southern belle and sister-in-law (and later wife) of his good friend Reverend John Bachman. Audubon recognized Maria’s innate talent in painting and tutored her in his method of painting “from nature.” In a short time, Martin progressed from a “skilled fancy worker who painted flowers on handicrafts to an accomplished botanical artist” (Lindsay 2018), and she also painted insects at a level of detail that rivaled that of Audubon. Maria Martin is credited with assisting on 24 different prints, of which five prints (Plates 198, 355, 359, 398, and 416) contain insects she painted. George Lehman was an accomplished landscape painter hired by Audubon to create the scenic backgrounds or detailed botanicals that acted as perches for the birds in 35 of Audubon’s prints. Only two of the prints to which Lehman contributed contain insects: one shows a paper wasp nest that hangs from the white oak branches the Canada jays are climbing on (Plate 107), and the other includes an uncolored beetle-esque form on the underside of a leaf, which is not present in the original watercolor and appears to have been added by the engraver Robert Havell, Jr. Havell was the final engraver for all of the Audubon prints and a talented landscape artist in his own right. As the engraver, he had a great influence on the prints’ ultimate composition and presentation. In fact, when I compared the original paintings Audubon gave to Havell for engraving with the final prints Havell produced, it was evident that Havell had a discernable influence on 168 (39%) of the prints. Havell’s influence ranged from the mundane—altering the composition, adding a small visual element, adding or subtracting background elements—to adding a new bird to the composition. In Mississippi Kite (Plate 117), Audubon instructed Havell to add a female version of the kite to the print by copying it from a print by Alexander Wilson, a competing ornithological artist of the time. In The Birds of America, Audubon envisioned that he was going to accurately portray every bird species in America, which seemed plausible at the time, given that the United States consisted of only about 25 states. To achieve his goal, Audubon traveled and collected bird and plant specimens all along eastern North America, from the Labrador coast in Canada south to Key West in Florida. Audubon found that the most productive areas of collecting were along the Mississippi and Ohio river waterways, where more than 325 bird species are known to migrate that flyway yearly. He travelled frequently on the river from his home in Henderson, Kentucky, to New Orleans, Louisiana. Following the business model of Victorian novels of the time, Audubon serialized his Birds of America as a subscription service: every couple of months, the subscriber would receive five hand-colored engravings—one large engraving, one medium-sized engraving, and three small engravings in a set. Because all of the birds were drawn “the size of life” as Audubon required, the large engravings included birds such as eagles, pelicans, egrets, cranes, swans, and flamingos. Even with the double elephant folio-sized paper, Audubon had to creatively pose the long necks of the flamingo (Plate 431) and anhinga (Plate 316) in oddly serpentine fashions to get them to fit on the page. Medium-sized engravings included ducks, egrets, kestrels, crows, and other crow-sized birds. The small engravings were mostly of smaller passerine birds, but occasionally would include medium-sized birds like a tern or plover. Audubon’s subscription, unlike the Victorian novels of the time, was aimed solely at wealthy individuals, heads of state, universities, and those of royal heritage. It is believed there were 180–200 complete sets sold (Steiner 2003), but the actual final number is challenging to discern, because many individuals joined and quit the subscription during its 12-year run. Originally Audubon planned for the series to comprise 400 prints, with each print representing a single species in a natural life-like pose among species-specific vegetation. As the project progressed, Audubon strove to make his work the definitive bird study. By collaborating with Havell, he increased the project to 435 prints, which allowed Audubon to include the new birds being collected from the western territories. When completed, The Birds of America included 1,065 individual birds drawn to life-size, which represented 489 different bird species. Audubon’s goal was to create a lifelike portrait of each of his bird subjects, a portrait that was more than a scientifically accurate representation of the bird—its form, color, and dimensions—but that also portrayed the bird in its natural environment exhibiting natural behaviors and, to a certain extent, its personality. Audubon also wanted to accurately represent the bird in its natural habitat surrounded by appropriate plants and other non-avian animals. Audubon included other vertebrate animals in his portraits, like small mammals, fish, and other birds that had fallen prey to raptors. When reptiles such as snakes, lizards, and alligators were represented, they were prey for birds or they might be eating birds themselves. Because insects and other arthropods are an important food source for many bird species, it is not surprising that they are often represented in the prints created by Audubon. My survey of the original prints revealed 76 different terrestrial arthropods represented in 67 distinct plates (Supplemental Table, available at https://doi.org/10.1093/ae/tmz066). The level of detail and accuracy of those representations ranges from indistinct ghost blobs with clubbed antennae catching the attention of the female Kentucky warbler (Plate 38) to the cecropia and Io moths being chased by a whip-poor-will (Plate 82), rendered as accurately as one would expect to find in a modern-day field guide. Overall, there are 34 insects represented with enough detail to allow identification to species (Supplemental Table). Not surprisingly, large and colorful Coleoptera (n = 22) and Lepidoptera (n = 17) are most represented within the plates, followed by nearly equal examples of Diptera (n = 7), Hymenoptera (n = 8), and spiders (Araneae, n = 9). title: Functional response of Pardosa altitudis Tikader and Malhotra, Teragnatha maxillosa Thorell, Neoscona mukherjei Tikader and Theridion sp. to rice green leafhopper
venue: ORYZA- An International Journal on Rice
abstract: Laboratory experiments were performed to determine the functional response of visual hunting spider, Pardosa altitudis Tikader and Malhotra and web-building spiders, Teragnatha maxillosa Thorell, Neoscona mukherjei Tikader and Theridion sp. to 2nd and 3rd instar nymph of rice grasshopper. The functional response of P altitudis, T maxillosa, N mukherjei and Theridion sp. to the different density of 2nd and 3rd instar nymph of rice grasshopper was typically of Holling Type II with a steep initial rise in prey capture rates as the density increased. P altitudis consumption increased to 26.7 per day 2nd instar nymphs of rice grasshopper which was higher than that of N mukherjei (23.1), T maxillosa (22.4) and Theridion sp. (18.8). However, in case of 3rd instar nymph of rice grasshopper, the consumption of N mukherjei was increased to 21.2 per day which was higher than that of L. altitudus (20.4), T maxillosa (19.2) and Theridion sp. (16.2). The search rate of N mukherjei was not significantly higher than L. altitudes against 2nd instar nymph of rice green hopper and handing time of L. altitudes was significantly lowest as compared to N. mukherjei. In case of 3rd instar nymph of rice green hopper, the search rate of N mukherjei was significantly higher followed P altitudus, T maxillosa and Theridion sp. while the handing times of N mukherjei was not significantly higher than L. altitudes. The lowest search rate and highest handling time taken by Theridion sp. for both 2nd and 3rd instar nymph of rice grass hopper. The result suggested that P altitudis have potential for being effective biocontrol agents.

title: Field Guides are Lenses
abstract: Field Guides are Lenses Sam Pickering (bio) David L. Wagner , Caterpillars of Eastern North America. Princeton University Press, 2005. 512 pages. Illustrated. $60, $29.95 pb. Field guides are lenses. By directing and broadening vision, they increase appreciation and provoke thought. They can even determine the course of a life. Had Caterpillars of Eastern North America dropped from a Christmas tree during my first instar, I suspect I would have molted into a creature different from the bookworm and literary gadfly I became. I spent childhood summers on my grandfather's farm in Virginia. During nights I read the novels of Edgar Rice Burroughs. During days I roamed pasture and wood catching and studying creepers and crawlers. The only guide in Grandfather's study described the diseases of cattle. As a result my scrutiny of insects never progressed beyond astonishment. In any case summer's lease was always short, and in August I migrated back to Nashville and an apartment on West End Avenue. In Nashville books were easy to come by; bugs were difficult, even though I explored alleys, peering into backyard gardens, hoping to discover spiders, particularly my great love, the black-and-yellow Argiope. For adults whom the racket of television and the internet has reduced to melancholy, field guides can be therapeutic. Opening a guide is comparable to stepping through the wardrobe in C. S. Lewis's Narnia books. Beyond the title page lie fabulous unimagined and unimaginable worlds. For ramblers, especially that genus known as nature writer, guides are essential. Not only do guides blaze trials for writers to follow, but, like markers beside paths, they determine what and how writers see, thus becoming unacknowledged [End Page 136] foundations supporting signatures of verbs and nouns. Two nights ago Vicki made fish chowder. Dinner was late, so I wandered the side meadow below the kitchen porch. That afternoon I'd finished reading Caterpillars of Eastern North America. I should have stayed inside and started this review, but David Wagner's book has a magical levitating power, and almost without thinking, I was outside, my fingers wrapping a lens. On a red maple I discovered two Saddled Prominents, caterpillars I had not seen previously, a sight almost as rich as Vicki's chowder, thick with haddock, lobster, and scallops. The insects were minute, one green, the other reddish, white spilling down their backs like melted marshmallows, the edges of the saddles brown, seared like the sides of marshmallows held low over a fire. Before sitting down to dinner, I saw a feast of caterpillars: White Spring Moth on mountain ash; Fall Web Worms on alder; and White-Marked Tussocks on almost every shrub. I could not identify the caterpillar of a dagger moth I found on both bay and wild raisin. Perhaps it was an early instar of the Impressive Dagger. The caterpillar's body was black and velvety, and yellowish hair (setae) burst from it in tufts. Its spiracles were white—these being openings along the insect's abdomen that allow it to breathe. Below the holes the caterpillar's body puffed out into a rack of red warts looking like purses. Field guides curb appetites and transform the harassed husband into that sane creature, the dawdler. Alas, the first words Vicki said on my appearing in the kitchen were more pointed than the soft nothings of a blessing. When she first called me, I was looking at a clutch of eggs on a willow leaf, sixteen tiny eggs deposited in a U. The eggs resembled amphora. Circling the brim of each egg was a silvery wheel, fourteen spikes jutting out from each hub. I don't know what insect laid the eggs, but I am going to watch them closely in hopes of finding out. The prospect excites me. How odd that things so small, so ostensibly removed from life as depicted on screens, can fill a day, making interest sizzle. Guides have an ancient history, some of their pages fabulous and fictional, decorated with sketches of the cockatrice and griffon, for example. Other pages have been utilitarian, for instance, fifteenth- and sixteenth-century herbals, which incidentally make fine evening reading, seeding dreams with words...

title: Goniurosaurus wuzhengjuni Chen & Chen 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Goniurosaurus wuzhengjuni Chen & Chen sp. nov. Figs 2, 3 Type materials. Holotype. • GXNU 2025101603, adult male (Fig. 2 A), from Baishou Nature Reserve, Yongfu County, Guilin City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China (25.0636°N, 109.7391°E; elevation 323 m a. s. l.) collected by H. L. Chen on 26 October 2025. Paratypes. • Three adult females GXNU 2025090812 (Fig. 2 B), GXNU 2025101601 (Fig. 2 C) – 02 (Fig. 2 D), same data to the holotype. Diagnosis. Goniurosaurus wuzhengjuni sp. nov. can be distinguished from its congeners through a distinct combination of morphological characteristics: (1) SVL 92.3–109.3 mm; (2) 0–1 internasals; (3) 2 gular scales bordering the internasals; (4) 8–9 gular scales bordering the postmentals; (5) 26–27 paravertebral tubercles between limb insertions; (6) 23 precloacal pores in males; (7) 7 nasal scales surrounding the nostril; (8) 9–10 sublabials; (9) 47–54 eyelid fringe scales or ciliaria; (10) 11–12 granular scales surrounding dorsal tubercles; (11) 21–22 dorsal tubercle rows at midbody and (12) 101–108 midbody scale rows; (13) 2 postcloacal tubercle present on each side; (14) a light yellow dorsal ground coloration on the head, body, and limbs covered with dense, irregular black blotches. Description. Holotype. GXNU 2025101603, adult male; SVL 92.3 mm; TaL 74.8 mm; AG 36.6 mm; SE 10.6 mm; EE 9.2 mm; HW 17.8 mm; HL 25.5 mm; SVL / AG 2.52; SVL / HL 3.62; HL / HW 1.43; SE / EE 1.15. The head is wider than the neck and dorsally covered with uniform granular scales interspersed with small tubercles. The rostral scale is convex and wider than high, bordered laterally by the first supralabial and prenasal scales, and posteriorly by the supranasal scale. Each external naris is encircled by seven nasal scales — anteriorly by the prenasal, dorsally contacting the supranasal and one granular scale (noted on the right side), and posteriorly by two smaller granular scales (Fig. 3 C). There are nine rectangular supralabials on each side (9 / 9). The eyes are relatively large with vertical pupils. A suborbital skin fold extends posteroventrally across the angle of the jaw. The tympanum is deeply recessed and bordered anteriorly by two spinose scales. The mental scale is bordered laterally by the first infralabials and posteriorly by four postmentals. There are ten rectangular infralabials on each side (10 / 10). The neck is narrower than the body. Dorsal body tubercles are each surrounded by 11 or 12 granular scales. There are 21–22 rows of dorsal tubercles at midbody, and 26–27 paravertebral tubercles between limb insertions. The body is relatively slender, bearing 101–108 granular scales around midbody. Larger ventral scales transition abruptly to smaller granular scales just anterior to the vent. There are 23 precloacal pores arranged in a continuous transverse series that does not extend onto the proximal thighs (Fig. 3 F). Two enlarged postcloacal tubercles are present laterally at the vent level. The limbs are long and slender; dorsally they bear granular scales and closely spaced tubercles, while ventrally, the scales are flat, ranging from juxtaposed to subimbricate. The hindlimbs are larger than the forelimbs. The dorsal surfaces of both manus and pes bear granular scales, with the pes bearing several conical tubercles. The ventral surfaces of the limbs are covered with large granular scales. Subdigital lamellae counts are as follows: 13 / 13 on the first finger, 19 / 17 on the fourth finger, 13 / 12 on the first toe, and 25 / 24 on the fourth toe. The original tail is slender at the base, gradually thickening towards the middle, and tapering to a blunt tip, bearing six distinct bands along its length. Coloration in life. The head, body, and limbs exhibit a grayish-white dorsal ground color with dense, irregular black blotches, some of which are partially fused on the head. The iris is orange. A pale-yellow nuchal loop is present, with a rounded posterior margin. Three pale-yellow bands occur on the body between the limb insertions and a postsacral band is located at the base of the tail. The ventral surfaces of the head, body, and limbs are white. The original tail bears a black ground color with distinct white bands, whereas the regenerated tail shows irregular white markings that coalesce toward its tip. Comparisons. Goniurosaurus wuzhengjuni sp. nov. is assigned to the G. luii group by a unique combination of morphological characteristics — more than 16 precloacal pores in males, claws encased in scales, and a slender, splayed body and limbs — consistent with the original definition of the group. The new species differs from its sister taxon, G. araneus, by having fewer eyelid fringe scales (CIL, 47–54 vs. 61–67), fewer scales around midbody (MB, 101–108 vs. 129–147), fewer subdigital lamellae under the fourth toe (LT 4, 17–19 vs. 23–24), and more precloacal pores (PP, 23 vs. 18–22). Additional scalation characters further emphasize the distinctiveness of G. wuzhengjuni sp. nov., as shown by the following combination of traits: (1) fewer MB (101–108 in G. wuzhengjuni vs. 123–151 in G. gezhi, 119–137 in G. chengzheng, 119–144 in G. luii Grismer, Viets & Boyle, 1999, 118–129 in G. huuliensis Orlov, Ryabov, Nguyen, Nguyen & Ho, 2008, 122–128 in G. kwangsiensis Yang & Chan, 2015, 112–127 in G. catbaensis Ziegler, Truong, Schmitz, Stenke & Rösler, 2008 and 127–129 in G. liboensis Wang, Yang & Grismer, 2013); (2) a different number of PP (23 in G. wuzhengjuni vs. 18–20 in G. gezhi, 20 in G. chengzheng, 16–21 in G. catbaensis and 25–28 in G. huuliensis); (3) fewer LT 4 (17–19 in G. wuzhengjuni vs. 23 in G. chengzheng, 21–24 in G. luii, 22–27 in G. kwangsiensis, 22–24 in G. catbaensis and 23–26 in G. liboensis); (4) distinct CIL counts (47–54 in G. wuzhengjuni vs. 57–61 in G. luii and 41–44 in G. huuliensis); and (5) more SBL (9–10 in G. wuzhengjuni vs. 6–8 in G. catbaensis). Detailed data are summarized in Table 2. G. wuzhengjuni sp. nov. differs from species of the G. lichtenfelderi group by having a more slender body and limbs, a greater number of subdigital lamellae under the first finger (11–13 vs. 6–10), and a broader black band either anterior or posterior to the three pale-yellow body bands. It is distinguished from the G. kuroiwae group by the presence of 23 precloacal pores in males (vs. absence in that group) and claws encased by four scales rather than unsheathed. The new species is further separated from the G. yingdeensis group by a greater number of precloacal pores. Variation. Measurements and scalation data for the type series are provided in Table 1. The paratypes generally conform to the holotype in coloration and overall morphological proportions, with the following exceptions: the ratio of snout – vent length to axilla – groin distance (SVL / AG) is 2.52 in the male (n = 1) and 2.19–2.21 in females (n = 3). Paratype GXNU 2025090812 differs from the remaining specimens in the following aspects: (1) the absence of an internasal scale, present in the others; (2) 11 granular scales surrounding the dorsal tubercles, compared to 12 in the others; and (3) 26 paravertebral tubercles between limb insertions, rather than 27 as in the others. Etymology. The specific epithet wuzhengjuni honors Professor Zhengjun Wu for his significant contributions to the study of Sauria. His research team pioneered the use of AI-based tail pattern recognition technology, which has greatly advanced the conservation and research of the nationally first-class protected species Shinisaurus crocodilurus, thereby supporting population-recovery efforts. The proposed common names are “ Wu’s Cave Gecko ” (in English) and “ 武氏睑虎 ” (wǔ shì jiǎn hǔ in Chinese). Distribution and ecology. Goniurosaurus wuzhengjuni sp. nov. was discovered in the karst regions of northern Guangxi, China, at elevations ranging from 280 to 351 meters in areas with dense arborous vegetation (Fig. 4 A). The species is nocturnal and was frequently observed on limestone surfaces near roadside slopes or around limestone accumulations at cave entrances (Fig. 4 B, C).

title: Inspired by nature: animals: the building/biology connection
abstract: Nature has always furnished stimulating ideas for the design of architecture, and the use of animal forms in contemporary architecture-whether to endow a project with symbolism, find a functional solution, or simply for aesthetic reasons-has become a commonplace practice. Inspired by Nature: Animals focuses on specific analogies, comparing and contrasting techniques and materials used in animal constructions with examples of human architecture. It gathers together the work of two dozen architects who have drawn on such structures as tortoise and snail shells, spiders' webs and birds' nests, beehives and beaver lodges. Among the built examples from around the world are inventive projects such as Elephant Skin House (PPAG Architects, Austria), Kiss the Frog! (mmw architects, Norway), Moore Apiary (Marlon Blackwell, Cashiers, North Carolina), Concrete Pod (Kazuya Morita Architecture Studio, Nagoya, Japan), and more, beautifully illustrated in colorful photographs supplemented by plans. The visual analogies underline how architects can find elegant solutions and create new, sustainable, and efficient architectonic forms by the close and understanding observation of nature.
