title: Washtub, Whelk, Widow, Woods
abstract: Just before dawn, we hear, through the window cracked open above the bed, an Eastern screech owl's tremolo. It is the only sound. So much is in it. Our limbs twine and warm and harden and soften. Maybe we've dreamt it, but no.I have just come back from a visit to my childhood home where my mother cares full-time for her mother, who, at ninety-seven, is getting used to a catheter, whose meat is cut up like a child's. Late August nasturtiums spilled from the metal washtub on the front porch, three shades of orange.This is not my house; it's his, and his kids’ when they're here, but they're with their mom this week and their beds are empty. The first sun is cool slate falling onto the world beyond the big window, onto poplar and mimosa and vine. How beautiful the moths that flap at this wide window at night, how scritchy and bandit-like the raccoons that come for his compost. Summer is turning toward fall. Fall will soon turn more deeply toward fall, the earlier dark, the winter caps pulled out. Before dreams let me go entirely, I have the sparse notion of a child of my own to whom I would give my too-big longjohns to wear with cap and coat on a winter walk. You, my child, are a tiny pinprick of dawnlight in the universe, you who cannot fill a thimble, but your wind could set a big shirt to sail on a wash line.The letter I would write you about it—the owl's tremolo, the whinny that sometimes follows. The sound creates a habitable space in time, a shelter where I put down my thoughts. A sound like a refuge. So singular and lonesome and secret, so full and empty, like the sound the prophet Elijah waited for, holed up in his cave in Mount Horeb, the pre-dawn sound of God talking. There was a wild wind outside the cave, says the biblical text, and an earthquake, and a fire, but no voice. And then—a low whisper, a thin silence. This was the only sound, and Elijah wrapped his face in his coat and went to the cave's mouth to listen. But the part about the cave comes after the rain, which comes after the war, which comes after the widow, and it's the widow I want to write you about because hers is a story of homes that take us in for a time, as he has done for me, as I have done for him, given shelter.He and I rise from bed to coffee and work and soaked oats. When you're sheltered by another, you can sense what he has sheltered there before: the marriage, the babies born, the kill butchered and butterflied, and the many clots of buttered oatmeal. And I like to imagine the nasturtiums I saw in their bright gold burn, as I turned to go, sensing the world of their brief washtub home. They bent from noon heat toward the cooler portion of mountain evening. Their stems coiled and crept, broad leaves like wide open faces, spiced blooms like the prettiest paper. Mom had started seeds in trays at the windowsill in March, transplanted the leggy hopefuls in May. Rehomed to the tub, the nasturtiums could feel out the story of suds and lye, all the submerged blouses made unfamiliar there, and shapeless, until stuttered down washboard rungs and hung in the wind like small sails (sails again) on the line.My father's aunt Aggie gave them the washtub, along with their first wringer washer, in 1972. Mom filled it with dirt and flowers when a hole rusted into its floor. The nasturtiums reach out for present sun and know, even so, the summers long in their home's history, the dogs in the divots under our porch and Aggie's.Hear the hymns murmured from dry lips, curse the tobacco pouch forgotten and soaked, find the bits of sweet oat roll and venison baloney in the denim pocket running the washboard with the rest. The hummingbird comes to the orange flower face, this flower foreign and far from where it belongs (native to the tropics and subtropics, the Andes, not the Appalachians); still, the bird's long tongue and the nasturtium's deep spur meet together, shape to shape, need to need, the sucrose nectar extra sweet down deep in this bright flourish on porch steps. Groping along the tub's contours, the blooms may be blind, may be seeing.How these flowers spill lavishly from the tub's rim. I picture his wash taken from my drier, the clothes of his children, in the shelter I give him and them in return, my house twenty minutes from theirs. Lululemon Goodwill shorts, Adidas things, socks with and without pairs, training bras, they all spill onto the table. An abundance for the chore of folding and sorting. This tumble of unreadable shapes is made decipherable again only when filled with a body. I think of the spill of laundry and the spill of showy blooms yearning for evening—I loved looking at them as I turned to go, my mother framed for me by the screen door, like when I was a child boarding a school bus—when I first picture the widow. I picture her like the nasturtiums bending from noon heat toward the cool, though there were no blooming things in droughted Zarephath. No—in the widow's hot lap, only a few sticks for a stick fire to cook the last cake of flour and die.So odd, then, to want to write you of her shelter and respite. To write what might have come from the prophet's tenancy with the widow. To suggest it brought about a kind of happiness, and that the rain, when it later came, was a rinse revelatory of that happiness, rinsing away all the dust and hardness to show a supple thing. But first, to recount the stick fire and the last crumbs of meal.In the drought of the thin pages of I Kings 17, God said to Elijah: Hide yourself by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan, and the birds will care for you. Elijah thus knew meat torn from a small beast's belly by a raven's beak and delivered, like mama bird to nestling: Here is your meat, little one, in your yawning gullet, and now I must feed the others the leftover. Go lap water from the brook, and here the liver, a dark disc of iron. Elijah, childless, at times dreamt of a baby with a tiny curl of hand like a prawn, like a centipede coil, all those ions and the softchew skin, an intensified star warming the small breast. Maybe he dreamed a child because the ravens fed their nestlings after feeding him.When the brook dried up, God said to Elijah: Go to the widow of Zarephath and she will care for you. And there she was, at the gate of the city, starving and gathering sticks for a final fire. Bring me a little water, a little bread, he said. She said, All that I have can fit in my palm. He said, Bring me a cake of it and I swear the jar of flour won't deplete, the jug of oil won't drain until God sends the rain. She took him in. Each day she lifted the lid, and after so many days, she stopped doubting the perpetual enough.Since the jar never emptied, the prophet took a handful of meal to the ledge of the roof each morning to watch the dawn dream up the city and to feed the birds as thanks to their species. The man and woman smelled of earth and sweat, with no water to waste on the washtub. She pulled out her dead husband's few things for him, and he sensed in the clean clothes the other man's body and gait and voice. He filled the clothes. She beat their shirts and pants over rocks, scrubbed them with sand. To a stubborn stain, she took alum and soapwort, with spit for lather. But then she gave up and they wore their layer of dust like another garment and, without the chore of laundry, she had time to draw a magnolia border on the kitchen wall in gypsum and soot. He found a sap to stay it, like lacquer. She seasoned their cakes with nasturtium petals pressed some other year in a book. She pulled on his coat to seek sticks at night when it fell cool, and he read to her, scripture but also tales; he fixed the loose floorboard and the cracked cistern with the same multipurpose sealing sap. She sewed on buttons, mended his trousers which were perhaps her husband's, made corn-husk dolls for the girls from homes less lucky. For her boy she made a tiny clay structure to resemble the city at dawn which the prophet saw dreamed into day.And the boy. His chores were thought and play and making the beds and making sure the littlest birds got some grain and not only the proud ravens. Their time was slow, inhabited. The three of them—this odd family—sat listening together to the tremolo of the screech owl, near and invisible in crepuscular light. Just when they thought it was finished, it would sound again. Round and whole, from mate to mate, a message that light and dark are softly one. That dawn and dusk are doorways to each home you will know in time.I wonder, have you ever heard it? The tremolo? The steady trill like a washboard of song. And the whinny to follow? As if a horse head were softly thrown back in silhouette to shiver dust from its mane. The letter I am trying to write you about it—this the only sound. So much is in it.Before the hospice nurse arrives, my mother leaves the house barefoot to walk the cold-dew field of late summer, an acre or two of grass and garden and unkempt pine. It's cold but she goes, makes the loop and the loop along the fence, checks the spring box, heads back to the house to my grandmother. In this circumscribed time, Mom gently salves and wraps the bed wound on my grandmother's heel.And here is the nurse, Camille, pulling up, climbing the porch steps past the tub of nasturtiums to check vitals and pills. Then Cindy, a home health aide, coming to bathe my grandmother. In the bathroom, she says lift up the girls, meaning my grandmother's breasts, her near-century skin like paper in a paper garden within this home that is not my grandmother's home but is. They drive away, Camille and Cindy, Grandma's hair clean and still wet. She is swaddled in a flannel gown. These two women travel from home to home, box trailers and brick and whatever, making hospital corners with the clean sheets everywhere. They see to the bed wounds and catheters, they resupply bales of Depends. Unseen hands touch the tenderest parts in beds all across creation to say: Let me make you at home in your body that's grown strange to you. In this house foreign, temporary, this house you've lived in all your life but don't remember, this house of a distant relative, this house you've never seen before. A house so unfamiliar when the sunlight and shadow land in turns through the window as the wind hurries the clouds.In between visits, my grandmother naps, Mom walks the field barefoot, picks kale and beans and puts up a canner of peaches with Dad. They scald off the peelings and stack the warm halves in wide-mouth jars filled with sugar water like nectar.During my visit with my parents, I picked kale with Mom at dawn. There was a morning moon and a mist. She said our neighbor Mary isn't doing well and her four girls are putting her in a home where there's Bingo and macramé. Why not keep her in one of their houses, she said. Not everyone can do what you're doing, I said. But I wished it for Mary too. I thought of the nursing home my youth choir sang for on Sunday afternoons, a woman in the back rocking like a baby in the invisible arms of our hymns. I felt guilty because I never wanted to go. After singing, we kids would hold hands and run run run once outside, down the tiny hill by the institutional walls, the grass never greener and our breath never quicker to come.On my drive back to my own house, and to his, I saw signs on the roadside for Foster families needed and I thought about it. I have that spare room. Why do they call them nursing homes instead of facilities, wards, barracks? Because they're homes. title: A trapdoor spider, Latouchia typica (Araneae: Halonoproctidae), uses vibrational cues as a trigger for predatory behavior
abstract: Spiders are one of the most dominant predators in terrestrial ecosystems.Although cues triggering predatory behavior in web-building and wandering spiders are well investigated, studies concerning burrowing species, the most ancestral group of spiders, are relatively limited.To clarify critical cues affecting the predatory behavior in burrowing species, we conducted vibration-reducing experiments using the trapdoor spider, Latouchia typica (Araneae: Ctenizidae), and nymphs of the speckled cockroach, Nauphoeta cinerea (Blattodea: Blaberidae), as prey.The spider achieved a high success rate of prey capture even in blindfolded conditions but reducing vibration with a rubber mat significantly decreased its predation success rate.In addition, the presence or absence of the blindfold did not affect the predation rates under the reducing vibration condition.These results indicate that substrate vibrations emitted from prey are critically important to trigger the predatory behavior in L. typica, but visual and chemical stimuli are not used even in the case when vibration cues are unavailable.This is the first report experimentally demonstrating the critical cues for predation in trapdoor spiders with vibration-reducing experiments.

title: FAMILY CTENIZIDAE • Trapdoor Spiders
abstract: This worldwide mygalomorph family includes 118 species. Most of the species are tropical in distribution. In North America north of Mexico we have 14 species in 4 genera. Ctenizids are the most famous of the trapdoor-building spiders. Most species build a thick, hinged door that they can hold tightly closed with their fangs by virtue of two tiny holes near the lip of the lid. When hunting, they wait under the slightly cracked opening, ready to pounce on any prey that wander within reach. After a lightning-fast capture, they return to the burrow and close the lid quickly. The snug-fitting lids of these spiders resemble a cork stopper and are sometimes referred to as cork doors. They are well camouflaged. The two species of the genus Cyclocosmia build thin doors. This large mygalomorph is a stocky brown spider with a dark shiny cephalothorax. The chelicerae have a rastellum. The fovea is U-shaped with the open end toward the rear; in Ummidia the U is open toward the front. The abdomen is lighter in color, gray, orange, or yellow. The legs are stocky.

title: Mygalomorph spiders from Peru (Araneae, Pycnothelidae, Rhytidicolidae): description of two new species and first Peruvian record of the family Rhytidicolidae
abstract: Two previously unknown mygalomorph spider species belonging to two families are described from the south-central Andean region of Peru. Within the family Pycnothelidae, Acanthogonatus goloboffi sp. n. is described, diagnosed and illustrated based on a female from Ccochirhuay, Cusco. The female of this species differs from most known Acanthogonatus by the shape of the spermathecae, which possess two single receptacles lacking additional projections or chambers. It further differs from congeners sharing a single receptacle by having non-spiraled ducts with a well-defined constriction and outwardly directed spherical receptacles. This represents the second record of the genus Acanthogonatus in Peru. Within the family Rhytidicolidae, Fufius agualaniensis sp. n. is described, diagnosed and illustrated based on a female from Agualani, Puno. The female of this species is distinguished from congeners by the following combination of characters: a straight fovea; a sternum as wide as long; a labiosternal junction with a well-developed septum; a preening comb on metatarsus IV consisting of seven large spines in a single row; and spermathecae with a wide, inwardly curved stalk giving rise to three sinuous branches ending in digitiform or domed structures. This constitutes the first formal record of the family Rhytidicolidae from Peru.

title: A diverse new spider (Araneae) fauna from the Jinju Formation, Cretaceous (Albian) of Korea
abstract: A collection of spiders from the Cretaceous (Albian) Jinju Formation of Korea is described. These finds increase the number of known spiders from the Jinju Formation from one to 11. There is considerable diversity of mygalomorphs and araneomorphs, including palpimanoids (including lagonomegopids), as well as cribellate and ecribellate entelegynes. Such diversity among so few specimens hints that an even greater range of families will come to light as more specimens are discovered in the future. The first non-amber Lagonomegopidae are described, with the first preservation of a spider eye tapetum in the fossil record, providing evidence for lagonomegopid enlarged eyes being posterior medians. The female-biased sex ratio of lagonomegopids is discussed and it is concluded that the bias is fortuitous. http://zoobank.org/urn:lsid:zoobank.org:pub:7926A54F-1B64-417E-91B4-027FAFCC8C0A

title: Indices of quality
abstract: Abstract A crucial distinction we have tried to draw has been between ‘indices’, signals that are reliable because they cannot be faked, and ‘handicaps’, signals that are reliable because they are costly to produce. The distinction is clear enough in a model, and there are examples that fall easily into one or other category. Fights between funnel-web spiders are settled in favour of the heavier spider if the weight difference is greater than about 10 per cent. A spider can signal its weight cost-free by vibrating the web. Female stalk-eyed fiies prefer males with long eye-stalks—eye-stalk length is associated with good condition, and hence with ‘good genes’, because it would be too expensive for low quality males to grow long eye-stalks. These are examples of an index, and a handicap, respectively.

title: Minerva: February 2000
abstract:
Early one November morning in southeast Queensland, a father found his baby son motionless and covered in vomit. He had puncture marks on the back of his right hand and a large black funnel web spider in his bed clothes (Medical Journal of Australia 1999;171:651-3). Four other people in the area have been poisoned by funnel web spiders since 1992. All recovered, but experts warn local hospitals to be ready for an increased incidence of bites as urban centres grow into the spiders' natural territory. The message is to keep antivenom in stock or know where to find it fast.

title: Hermachola capensis Ríos-Tamayo & Engelbrecht & Goloboff 2021, comb. nov.
abstract: Hermachola capensis (Ausserer, 1871), comb. nov. Figures 3E–H, 35A–F Brachythele capensis Ausserer, 1871: 175. Hermacha capensis (Ausserer): Benoit, 1964: 417 (after Simon, 1903: 906). MATERIAL EXAMINED: HOLOTYPE: South Africa: Western Cape Province: Cap der guten Hoffnung [Cape of Good Hope, 34°02′S 18°25′E], 1857, 1♀, 2 imm (ZMB 49057). REMARKS: The true provenance of the type specimen is uncertain as extensive collection of mygalomorphs on the Cape Peninsula by Purcell and Tucker at the turn of the 19th century, as well as more recent general arthropod surveys there using pitfall trapping, have failed to yield new material. Targeted surveys of mygalomorphs on the peninsula should be a priority to determine whether this species occurs there, as well as to collect fresh material of several other species previously recorded. DIAGNOSIS: Females of Hr. capensis can be distinguished from all other Hermachola species by their epigastric plate with a medial extension reaching the middle of the second pair of book lungs (fig. 35C, D) and a greater number of cheliceral denticles (>20, fig. 35F; fewer than 15 in Hr. crudeni and Hr. lyleae). The spermathecae are more elongated than in Hr. crudeni (fig. 35E, similar to Hr. lyleae). DESCRIPTION: FEMALE HOLOTYPE (ZMB 49057, figs. 3E–H, 35A–F): Total length: 14.24. Carapace (fig. 35A): length 5.47, width 4.05. Cephalic region: length 3.51, clypeus small with 4 marginal bristles; 3 bristles in front of the OQ. Fovea: small, width 0.49, straight. Ocular measurements: AME 0.13, ALE 0.28, PME 0.20, PLE 0.22, OQ length 0.45, width 0.95; AME-ALE 0.09, PME-PLE 0.00, AME-PME 0.07, ALE-PLE 0.04, AME-AME 0.09, PME-PME 0.42. Chelicerae (fig. 35F): length 3.45, width 2.06; with retrodorsal bristles, no rastellum. Cheliceral furrow with 11 promarginal teeth and 24 mesobasal denticles. Labium: length 0.40, width 0.93. Palpal endites: length 1.96, width 0.88, with 25 cuspules on inner corner, prolateral face straight, soft area small, with long uniformly distributed setae. Sternum (fig. 35B): length 2.55, maximum width 2.32. Abdomen (fig. 35C, D): length 6.02, with a covering of fine setae and longer emergent setae. PMS: length 0.65; PLS: length of basal:medial:apical segments 1.00:0.84:0.85; total length 2.69. Lengths of legs and palp: I: 3.89, 2.30, 2.90, 2.72, 1.66, 13.47. II: 3.50, 2.09, 2.54, 2.48, 1.57, 12.18. III: 3.07, 1.70, 1.91, 2.71, 1.42, 10.81. IV: 3.98, 2.10, 2.96, 3.89, 1.56, 14.49. Palp: 2.79, 1.60, 1.78, —, 2.02, 8.19. Chaetotaxy: Leg I: femur, 1 PA; patella, 0; tibia, 1-1 p, 1-1-2 v; metatarsus, 2-1-0-2 V; tarsus, 0. Leg II: femur, 1 PA; patella, 0; tibia, 1-1 P, 1-1-3 V; metatarsus, 1 P, 2-2-0-2 V; tarsus, 0. Leg III: femur, 1-1 PA, 1 RA; patella, 1 P, 1-1 R; tibia, 1 P, 1-1 D, 1-1 R, 2-2-3 V; metatarsus, 1-1-1 P, 1-1-1 D-R, 1-1-1 R, 2-2-3 V; tarsus, 0. Leg IV: femur, 1-1-1 d; patella, 1 p; tibia, 1-1-1-1 P, 2-2-3 V; metatarsus, 1-1 P, 1-1-1 D-P, 1-1-1 D-R, 1-1-1 R, 2-2-3 V; tarsus, 0. Palp: femur, 1 P A; patella, 0; tibia, 1-1 P, 2-2-4 V; tarsus, 1 PB. Spermathecae: coiled with 3 loops, terminal receptacle oriented inward (fig. 35E). Scopulae: Metatarsi: I, dense, uniformly distributed; II, sparse 2:3A; III–IV, 0. Tarsi: I–II, dense, uniformly distributed (II divided by band of bristles); III–IV, 0, with ventral bristles uniformly distributed. Trichobothria: Tibiae: palp 9-9; I 10-10; II 10-8; III 8-10; IV 10-9. Metatarsi: I (3)1(2)1(4)1; II (4)1(1)1(2)1(4)1; III (5)1(2)1(2)1(4)1; IV (4)1(2)1(3)1(4)1. Tarsi: palp 12; I–II 14; III–IV 13. Preening combs: III 2 PV-3 RV; IV 3 PV-3 RV. Color in alcohol: Overall yellowish red (chelicerae darker); legs like carapace. Abdomen light yellowish (likely a result of long term preservation); spinnerets yellowish. MALES: Unknown. DISTRIBUTION: South Africa: Western Cape Province: Known only from the type locality, but see Remarks above. The original description indicated “Cap der guten Hoffnung,” which corresponds to the history of the Novara Expedition that visited the port of Cape Town (Organ, 2007).

title: Idiommata scintillans
abstract: Idiommata scintillans (Rainbow & Pulleine, 1918) Common name: South Australian Silverback Fig. 2a–e Lampropodus scintillans Rainbow & Pulleine, 1918: 135, plate 17, figs 17–20, plate 1, figs 21–22, plate 23, figs 84, 85. Idiommata iridescens: Main, 1985: 13. Type. Lectotype ♂ of Idiommata scintillans, SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Black Hill, Mt Lofty Ra [34.703°S 139.457°E, Google] Adelaide, 18.XI.1917, AM KS5191, examined. Diagnosis. Males differ from those of I. blackwalli in the short, domed upper spur on tibia I (Fig. 2d). Tibial spur dorsally concave, megaspine shorter than prodorsal one. Prolateral process about as long as basal width and a short triangular stub, much shorter than slightly curved spine. Lyra with about 10 spatulate setae. Males with two rows of teeth on paired claws of all legs; males with dense matt of silver hairs on carapace and golden hairs on abdomen. Description. Lectotype ♂, AM KS5191. Carapace 9.46 long, 8.15 wide. Abdomen 8.70 long, 7.44 wide. Leg measurements: I: 8.33; 4.67; 6.00; 6.00; 3.67; 28.67. II: 8.00; 4.33; 5.50; 6.00; 3.17; 27.00. III: 7.17; 4.00; 5.17; 6.50; 3.33; 26.17. IV: 9.67; 6.00; 7.33; 9.50; 2.83; 35.33. Palp: 5.25; 2.92; 3.50; 2.33; 14.00. Colour in alcohol. Carapace, chelicerae and legs reddish brown. Abdomen entirely brown with dense pile of golden hairs. Carapace. Very densely covered with pile of white hairs so dense as to obscure cuticle and margins and mixed with uniform covering of brown bristles. Fovea short, slightly procurved. Eyes. Group: head width, 0.32; eye group front, back, long, 51: 79: 71. Back row procurved. Sizes: AME: ALE: PME: PLE, 25: 22: 22: 24; MOQ front, back, long, 53: 59: 45; Interspaces: AME–AME 0.4; AME–ALE 0.5; ALE–PLE 2.0; PME–PME 1.4; PME–PLE 0.0. Chelicerae. Entire dorsal and lateral surface covered with long brown bristles and few hairs. Rastellum absent. Promargin of furrow with 8 spaced teeth, basomesally with 1 or 2 granules. Peg setae absent. Ridge below dorsal edge of chelicerae on inner face absent. Labium 1.77 wide, 0.69 long. Maxillae 2.69 long in front, 3.46 long behind, 1.23 wide; with 3–7 blunt cuspules on inner angle; lyra consists of 5 thick ectal and 6–7 smaller ental spathulate setae in line set close to ventral edge. Sternum 4.61 long, 4.23 wide; separated from labium by two broad, fused sigilla; posterior and middle sigilla circular, 0.23 long and close to or touching margin; anterior sigilla not discernible. Legs. Dense fringes of hair on all retrolateral femora (as in Zidiommata simonmaraisi sp. nov., Fig 10e but retrolaterally). Scopula distribution: entire on metatarsi I, and on tarsi I–III; divided on tarsi IV; divided and in distal 2/3 (II) or 1/4 (III, IV) on metatarsi II–IV. Tibia I with stout curved spur with short straight megaspine; prolaterally with straight megaspine and dorsal cuticular stub (Fig. 2d). Preening combs absent. Spines. Leg I: fe, p3 d3; pa, 0; ti, p2 v2 + megaspine; me, v1. Leg II: fe, p6 d2; pa, 0; ti, p4 v5; me, p2 v1. Leg III: fe, p2 d2 r3; pa, r1; ti, p2 r1 v4; me, p3 r3 v9. Leg IV: fe, p2 d2 r2; pa, r1; ti, p3 r5 v10; me, p3 r4 v16. Palp: fe, p1; pa, 0; ti, p3–4 v1. Claws. STC I with two juxtaposed rows, each of four teeth; STC IV with one tooth on each margin: tooth long on inner margin, very small on outer. Trichobothria. tibia, ca. 15 per row; metatarsi, ca. 17; tarsi, a broad band of ca. 30. Spinnerets. PMS torn away; base scars 0.23 in diameter and PLS 1.38, 0.46, 0.23, 2.07. Palp. No dense brushes of hair on femora. Bulb pyriform with two distal spiralled keels on embolus (Fig. 2a, b). Distribution and habitat. Known only from Mt Lofty Ranges, South Australia. In 2000, on an Australian Heritage Commission funded survey I conducted of mygalomorphs in all Australian natural history museums, I reported no Idiommata specimens from the Mt Lofty Ranges. Other material examined. title: Yunka Duperre & Tapia 2026, gen. nov.
abstract: Yunka Dupérré & Tapia gen. nov. Type species. Yunka suenos Dupérré & Tapia, sp. nov. Etymology. The generic epithet is a noun, invariable, taken from the Kichwa language “ yunka ” meaning from the coastal region, in reference to member of the genus being found in the Ecuadorian coastal region. The gender is feminine. Diagnosis. Males and females are distinguished from Cyclosternum, Cymbiapophysa and Tandayarachne by their undivided tarsal scopula on leg I-II (Fig. 21 E) (not from Cymbiapophysa otongachi and C. velox both have undivided tarsal scopula on leg I – II). Males are further distinguished by the combination of the following characters: tibial apophysis absent (Yunka baboso sp. nov., Fig. 30 E) if present, with ventral elongated branch bearing a short apical megaspine and long basal megaspine, dorsal branch reduced, with or without megaspine (Fig. 30 A – D) (in some cases, on the same specimen the dorsal megaspine was present on the left but absent on the right side), whereas tibial apophysis with ventral and dorsal branch of about equal size in Cyclosternum (Peñaherrera-R. et al. 2024 a: fig. 7), ventral branch longer than dorsal branch in Cymbiapophysa (Peñaherrera-R and Ghia 2025: fig. 5), Tandayarachne (Peñaherrera-R and Guayasamin 2025, fig. 13 B). Females are distinguished from Cyclosternum and Cymbiapophysa by their short dual spermathecae, L-shaped spermathecae or straight, with square to rectangle guard plates (Figs 23 A, 25 C, 29 A); whereas Cyclosternum and Cymbiapophysa with rounded, oval or triangular spermathecal head with triangular or elongated rectangular guard plates (Gabriel 2016: fig. 69; Peñaherrera-R. et al. 2024 a: fig. 14). Description. Medium to large mygalomorph spider (total length male, 23.90–31.38; total length female 34.45–39.62); carapace elongate oval; pars cephalica flat, fovea straight (Fig. 19 B, 22 B); eyes on low mound. Labium excavated, with 10–42 cuspules; endites with 71–125 cuspules restricted to 13–19 % surface of the endites, anterior lobe moderately developed (Fig. 22 C, 26 C). Sternum longer than wide, labio-sternal mound joined or separated; anterior and median closer to margin, posterior one distant from margin (Fig. 22 C, 24 B). Males dorsally with abdominal urticating setae type Ia (Fig. 38 A) and Ib (Fig. 38 B); females dorsally with type I (Fig. 38 D), and Ia (Fig. 38 C). Legs with undivided tarsal scopula on leg I – II (Fig. 21 E); metatarsal scopula present on all legs. Males with tibial apophysis absent or if present, with ventral elongated branch bearing a short apical megaspine and long basal megaspine, dorsal branch reduced, with or without megaspine. Male palpal tibia straight, without spines retolaterally, with spines prolaterally and dorsally (Figs 20 A, 20 B, 27 A, 27 B); cymbium bilobed with small retrolateral apophysis (Fig. 30 F – H); bulb with narrow, elongated embolus; tegular heel large; with elongated PS smooth, disjunct and reaching lower half and curving and reaching upper half; PI long, reaching below lower half, smooth to serrated apically, disjunct medially; short converging EK; elongated SA, reaching below lower half, serrated to undulate forming a large ventral plate (Figs 7 D, 20 C, 20 D, 31 A – F). Females with L-shaped or barbell-shaped spermathecae, with slight constriction, square to rectangle guard plates (Figs 23 B, 25 D, 29 B); spermathecal head oval to mushroom shape; guard plates rectangular to square, fused to separated (Figs 23 B, 23 D, 29 D). Composition. Yunka suenos sp. nov., Yunka guasaganda sp. nov. and, Yunka baboso sp. nov. Distribution. Ecuador.

title: Hermacha sericea Purcell 1902
abstract: Hermacha sericea Purcell, 1902 Figures 2H, 4M–P, 14A–F, 15A–J, 16A–E Hermacha sericea Purcell, 1902: 375. MATERIAL EXAMINED: HOLOTYPE: South Africa: Northern Cape Province: Van Rhyns Dorp Div. and the western part of the Calvinia Div., August, 1897, M. Mally, 13 (SAM-ENWX003666). PARATYPES: South Africa: Northern Cape Province: Williston, 44 km WNW, Loskop, 3.9 km WNW; near BioGaps site 3110_2030 (31°13′27.14″S 20°28′36.52″E), April, 2017, I. Engelbrecht, S. Mitchell, C. Sole, T. Majelantle, 1♀ (NCA 2017 /1868); Same data, 1♀ (NCA 2017 /1869). REMARKS: Copulatory bulbs of the male holotype (SAM-ENW-X003666) are broken (fig. 15D, E); copulatory bulb measurements are taken from the male SAM-ENW-C008684 (figs. 4M, N, 15I, J). DIAGNOSIS: Males of H. sericea can be distinguished by the long copulatory bulb (Rlw ~2.5, figs. 15D, E, I, J). Differs from H. nigrispinosa, H. montana, and H. tuckeri by having a small apical flange on the embolus (figs. 4N, 15I) (long flange in H. nigrispinosa [fig. 12D], without flanges in H. montana [fig. 9D, E], and with two flanges in H. tuckeri [fig. 18E]). Females can be distinguished by the spermathecae (fig. 16E), which differ from H. evanescens and H. lanata in the smaller apical receptacle. DESCRIPTION: MALE HOLOTYPE (SAM-ENW-X003666, figs. 2H, 4M–P, 14A–F, 15A–J): Total length: 10.93. Carapace (fig. 14A): length 5.22, width 3.91, with lateral dark marginal bristles, and dorsal pubescence. Cephalic region: length 3.15; clypeus almost absent, with 5 bristles on the edge, some bristles in front and back of the OQ. Fovea: width 0.33, short, procurved. Ocular measurements: AME 0.13, ALE 0.31, PME 0.19, PLE 0.21, OQ length 0.54, 0.91 width; AME-ALE 0.08, PME-PLE 0.00, AME-PME 0.06, ALE-PLE 0.10, AME-AME 0.17, PME-PME 0.40. Chelicerae (fig. 14D): length 2.83, width 1.60, with dark retrodorsal bristles, rastellum formed by many strong setae; intercheliceral tumescence small, pallid with setae. Cheliceral furrow with an irregular line of 8 (5-1-2) promarginal teeth and 3 mesobasal denticles. Labium: length 0.27, width 0.77. Palpal endites: length 1.75, width 0.85, with 22 cuspules on inner corner, prolateral face straight, soft area long, with long uniformly distributed hairs. Sternum (fig. 14B): length 2.56, maximum width 2.14. Abdomen (fig. 14C): length 5.45, covered with small hair and bristles. PMS: length 0.57; PLS: length of basal:medial:apical segments 1.04:0.79:0.82; total length 2.65. Lengths of legs and palp: I: 4.24, 2.48, 3.27, 2.92, 2.02, 14.93. II: 4.05, 2.15, 2.80, 2.95, 2.15, 14.10. III: 3.60, 1.82, 2.26, 3.56, 2.18, 13.42. IV: 4.55, 2.11, 3.54, 4.48, 2.37, 17.05. Palp: 2.50, 1.35, 1.89, —, 1.06, 6.80. Chaetotaxy: Leg I: femur, 1 PA, 1-1-1 D, 1 RA; patella, 1-1 P; tibia, 1-1 P, 3-4-2 V, and a strong apical spine (ventral posterior, figs. 4P, 14E, F); metatarsus, 1 P (1:2 B), 2-0-1 V, slightly curved (1:3 B, fig. 2H); tarsus, 0. Leg II: femur, 1-1 P, 1-1-1 D, 1-1-1 R; patella, 1-1 P; tibia, 1-1 P, 1-2-1-2 V; metatarsus, 1 P, 2-0-2 V; tarsus, 0. Leg III: femur, 1-1-1 P, 1-1 D (1:2 B), 1-1-1 R; patella, 1-1 P, 1 R; tibia, 1-1 P, 1 D, 1-1-1 R, 2-2-3 V; metatarsus, 1-1-1 P, 1-1 D-P (1:2 A), 1-1-1 D-R, 2-2-3 V; tarsus, 0. Leg IV: femur, 1-1-1 P, 1-1-1 D, 1-1-1 R; patella, 1 R; tibia, 1-1 P, 1-1 R, 2-2-1-2 V; metatarsus, 1-1-1 P, 1-1-1 D-P, 1-1-1 D-R, 2-1-2-3 V; tarsus, 0. Palp (figs. 4O; 15A–C, F–H): femur, 1 P A; patella, 0; tibia, 2-2 P, 1-1 R, 1-2 V; tarsus, 6 A (fig. 4O, 15C, H), with numerous small rigid bristles. Copulatory bulb: Embolus of both copulatory bulbs of the type specimen are broken (figs. 4M, N, 15D, E, I, J). The measurements taken are from the male SAM-ENW-C008684, length 2.35, width 0.94, Rlw 2.5; (fig. 15I, J). Scopulae: Metatarsi: I–II, dense (3:4 A); III–IV, sparse apical (prolateral, IV escarce setae). Tarsi: I–II, dense, uniformly distributed throughout the segment; III–IV, sparse, uniformly distributed (III divided by a narrow band of setae; IV, divided very wide band of setae with a line of setae on both sides of the band of setae). Trichobothria: Tibiae: I 10-10; II 11-10; III 11-10; IV 12-11. Metatarsi: I 1(5)1(3)1(2)1(1)1(6); II 1(4)1(3)1(2)1(1)1(5); III 1(5)2(4)1(2)1(6); IV 1(4)1(2)1(2)1(1)1(5). Tarsi: I 25; II 23; III 25; IV 26. Color in alcohol: Overall reddish yellow, legs like carapace (tarsi pallid ventrally), chelicerae darker. Abdomen yellowish with pallid mottling; spinnerets pallid yellowish. FEMALE (NCA 2017/1868, fig. 16A–E): Total length: 13.42. Carapace (fig. 16A): length 5.02, width 3.81. Cephalic region: length 3.23, clypeus small with 6 marginal bristles; 9 bristles in front of the OQ and 5 posterior (between PME-PME). Fovea: width 0.51, procurved. Ocular measurements: AME 0.13, ALE 0.34, PME 0.23, PLE 0.30, OQ length 0.61, width 0.99; AME-ALE 0.08, PME-PLE 0.03, AME-PME 0.11, ALE-PLE 0.09, AME-AME 0.18, PME-PME 0.43. Chelicerae (fig. 16D): length 3.49, width 2.18; with retrodorsal dark bristles, rastellum numerous strong bristles. Cheliceral furrow with an irregular line of 8 (4-4) promarginal teeth and 4 mesobasal denticles. Labium: length 0.39, width 0.97. Palpal endites: length 1.87, width 0.97, with 36 cuspules on inner corner, prolateral face slightly curved, soft area large, with long uniformly distributed hairs. Sternum (fig. 16B): length 2.55, maximum width 2.15. Abdomen (fig. 16C): length 6.06, with small hair and bristles covering. PMS: length 0.70; PLS: length of basal:medial:apical segments 1.10:0.85:0.81; total length 2.76. Lengths of legs and palp: I: 3.70, 2.37, 2.34, 2.14, 1.69, 12.24. II: 3.38, 2.17, 2.10, 2.06, 1.68, 11.39. III: 2.98, 1.74, 1.63, 2.50, 1.87, 10.72. IV: 3.82, 2.10, 2.87, 3.54, 1.78, 14.11. Palp: 2.62, 1.48, 1.53, —, 1.66, 7.29. Chaetotaxy: Leg I: femur, 1 PA, 1-1-1-1-1 d; patella, 0; tibia, 1 P, 1-2 V; metatarsus, 2-2 V; tarsus, 0. Leg II: femur, 1 PA, 1-1-1-1-1 d; patella, 0; tibia, 1-1 P, 2-2 V; metatarsus, 1 P, 2-2 V; tarsus, 0. Leg III: femur, 1 ra, 1-1-1-1 d; patella, 1-1 P, 1 R; tibia, 1-1 P, 1 D, 1-1 R, 2-3 V; metatarsus, 1-1-1 P, 1-1-1 D-P, 1-1-1 D-R, 2-2-3 V; tarsus, 0. Leg IV: femur, 1-1-1-1 d with PA patch of small rigid setae; patella, 0, with D-P patch of small rigid setae; tibia, 1-1 R, 2-2 V; metatarsus, 1-1 P (1:2 A), 1 D-P (A), 1-1-1 D-R, 2-1-1-1-3 V; tarsus, 0. Palp: femur, 1 P A; patella, 0; tibia, 2 P, 4 V; tarsus, 2 VB. Spermathecae: narrow base and a sligthly rounded apical receptacle (fig. 16E). Scopulae: Metatarsi: I–II, dense, uniformly distributed; III, sparse, asymetric (1:2 A, only P); IV, sparse A (only P). Tarsi: I–II, dense, uniformly distributed; III–IV, sparse, uniformly distributed (III divided by a narrow band and IV by a wide band of setae, and presence of a line of setae on both sides of the central band). Trichobothria: Tibiae: palp 9-9; I 11-11; II 10-10; III 12-11; IV 13-12. Metatarsi: I (4)1(0)2(1)1(1)1(2)1; II (5)1(2)1(0)1(2)1(3)1; III (4)1(0)1(1)1(0)1(2)1; IV (5)1(0)1(1)1(0)1(1)1(2)1. Tarsi: palp 21; I 27; II 25; III 26; IV 28. Color in alcohol: Overall yellowish brown, legs like carapace. Abdomen brown, with large dark anterior spot and posterior dark bands (fig. 16C); ventral surface light; spinnerets like ventral surface. ECOLOGY: The specimens collected on the farm Loskop near Williston were found in the Western Upper Karoo vegetation type of the Nama Karoo Biome. The soil was relatively compact, typical yellow clayey loam derived from shale, with a loose covering of fine grey gravel. One of the specimens was located in a closed burrow while soil scraping for trapdoor spiders. The top of the burrow was located in a small depression in the soil surface, and when opened the burrow walls contained a very thick, papery silk lining. The second specimen was found with an open burrow with a distinctive round entrance, as in H. evanescens. ADDITIONAL MATERIAL EXAMINED: South Africa: Northern Cape Province: Tankwa National Park, Renoster River (32°14.70′S 20°05.82′E, 490 m), July 10–August 17, 2014, S. van Noort, 13 (SAM-ENWC008801); same data, 13 (SAM-ENW-C008684). DISTRIBUTION: The type locality is imprecise and spans the northern part of the Western Cape Province and the adjacent part of the Northern Cape. The other localities are in the Northern Cape Province of South Africa. It appears that this species occurs in the western parts of the Karoo, and possibly the adjacent parts of Namaqualand.
